portfolios.title: Who Should Pay for Pollution? Corporate Responsibility and Climate Justice in Hong Kong

essay.text:
Who Should Pay for Pollution? Corporate Responsibility and Climate Justice in Hong Kong When I go shopping for clothes in Causeway Bay, I often come across T-shirts labelled as “sustainable”. At first, I viewed sustainable shopping as a straightforward way to reduce my environmental impact. However, after taking CCGL 9065, I now recognize that consumers cannot make fully informed decisions when companies control how environmental information is presented. This gap between what consumers believe they are buying and the hidden environmental costs of production needs to be addressed. I believe meaningful climate action requires not only individual efforts but also companies taking responsibility for their products' environmental impacts. Although the examples that will be discussed are global, Hong Kong's regulatory framework provides a useful perspective on strengthening corporate responsibility. Our Week 3 discussion of fashion and product life cycles showed that a product’s environmental impact does not end when consumers discard it. Life Cycle Assessment evaluates impacts across a product’s life, but its results depend on the system boundary defining which processes are included (International Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2006). H&M’s sustainability marketing illustrates the risk of greenwashing in the fashion industry. In 2022, Norway's Consumer Authority cautioned H&M that using the Higg Materials Sustainability Index to support environmental claims in garment marketing could be considered misleading, as such claims might not adequately represent a garment's overall environmental impact (Norwegian Consumer Authority, 2022). Recycled materials may reduce some impacts, but they do not themselves account for production, transportation, pollution, or disposal. The case shows how a sustainability label can conceal a wider footprint and prevent consumers from making informed purchasing decisions.

Hong Kong already has a framework that can be expanded. The Product EcoResponsibility Ordinance (Cap. 603) provides for Producer Responsibility Schemes, based on the “polluter pays” principle. Existing schemes cover plastic shopping bags, waste electrical and electronic equipment, and glass beverage containers. Under the glass-container scheme, suppliers must register, submit returns and audit reports, and pay a recycling levy (Environmental Protection Department [EPD], n.d.). In July 2025, the Legislative Council passed a common framework to facilitate PRSs for additional products (EPD, n.d.). Hong Kong should use this framework to introduce a textile scheme requiring producers to fund collection and recycling, with higher fees for products that are harder to reuse or recycle. Critics may argue that these costs raise product prices or burden small businesses. However, fees should reflect the difficulty of recycling different materials, rather than functioning as a flat tax. The goal is not to punish consumers, but to stop producers shifting disposal costs onto society. The same transfer of responsibility appears on a much larger scale in the fossil-fuel industry. InfluenceMap (2024) linked 57 corporate and state entities to approximately 80% of global CO₂ emissions from these industries between 2016 and 2022. More concerningly, ExxonMobil's scientists had produced projections that accurately anticipated global warming, while the company’s later public communications were inconsistent with its internal scientific knowledge (Supran et al., 2023). This connects to our Week 7 discussion of truth and manufactured doubt: when companies conceal what they know, the public is left to bear both the environmental consequences and the confusion. Hong Kong’s climate-disclosure rules are a useful start, but information must lead to accountability. From financial years beginning on or after 1 January 2025, all Main Board issuers must disclose Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions. Broader climate-related disclosures are being phased in, with mandatory reporting for large-cap issuers from 2026 (Stock Exchange of Hong Kong Limited [SEHK], 2024). Disclosure makes corporate

emissions more visible, but it does not itself pay for the damage. Therefore, Hong Kong should build on the polluter-pays principle by requiring major polluters to contribute to an independently monitored environmental remediation fund according to their verified emissions and waste. Such accountability would ensure polluters bear the costs of their actions and help finance environmental restoration and support affected communities. Ultimately, the problem is not that consumers do too little; it is that those with the greatest power to prevent pollution can shift its costs onto everyone else. Meaningful climate action cannot happen if major corporations continue to use narrow assessment boundaries, conceal their environmental footprint, and contribute to public doubt. From a Hong Kong perspective, extending producer responsibility to textiles and requiring major polluters to help finance environmental recovery are practical ways to address this problem. Climate action should not leave consumers carrying the burden alone. It must reach those with the power to design, produce and profit.

portfolios.title: Cooling for Climate Justice

essay.text:
A summer night in a Hong Kong subdivided flat can be hotter indoors than outdoors. In a survey of 31 Kwai Chung households, apparent indoor temperature reached 44°C after dark at relative humidity above 72 per cent; over 70 per cent reported heat-related symptoms, and 65 per cent avoided air-conditioning because of electricity costs (Ho, 2025). Indoor heat is thus a housing condition, not a meteorological event.

Approximately 220,000 people occupy 110,000 subdivided units (Ho, 2025), and the Observatory recorded 61 hot nights in 2021, the most since 1884 (Lai et al., 2026). Risk is spatially concentrated: building-level heat-health risk in Sham Shui Po ranges from 0.152 to 0.845 at night, peaking where overcrowding exceeds 400 per cent (Lai et al., 2026). The stakes extend beyond housing. Suicide claims an estimated 720,000 lives yearly, and temperature-attributable suicide is projected to rise most sharply in warmer regions, including Southeast Asia, partly through sleep disruption (Ro et al., 2026). This essay argues that Hong Kong should apply solar-reflective coatings to all subdivided-unit buildings by 2030, prioritising the highest-risk blocks, and finance the work through utility energy-efficiency funds rather than tenant charges.

Coatings modify building fabric rather than occupant behaviour, which matters where residents work long shifts and cannot alter ventilation or energy use. Alternatives are weaker. Rebuilding serves future rather than current occupants, and greening offers limited relief in dense tropical developments: an additional green park reduced Singaporean urban heat island intensity by 0.022°C, and green plot ratio correlated negatively with cooling (−0.45) (Aydin et al., 2025). Coatings instead raise solar reflectance, so less radiation is absorbed by the façade and re-emitted indoors (Wong, 2025).

Evidence exists at scale. A pilot across 88 Tampines blocks reduced ambient temperature by up to 2°C; it will extend to all HDB estates by 2030 at an additional S$60 million, with government funding the premium over conventional paint, and residents consumed less electricity as air-conditioning demand fell (Wong, 2025). Hong Kong has trialled passive radiative cooling paint and applied it to the Coliseum roof (Legislative Council, 2025); the constraint is coverage, not feasibility.

Coverage should be allocated by building rather than district, since the risk index identifies blocks exceeding the 400 per cent threshold (Lai et al., 2026), and delivered through existing mechanisms: CLP’s 50 million for 70,000 low-income households and HEC’s 1.2 million for 1,200 subdivided-unit households (Legislative Council, 2025). Support should be targeted, as over 70 per cent of EU measures were untargeted and the £150 Warm Home Discount proved “a drop in the ocean” (Croon & Lausberg, 2023, p. 4). One objection requires attention. Green–blue adaptation across 5,503 African municipalities raised housing prices 13.0 per cent and population 52.9 per cent; rent control alone intensified displacement pressure (0.377 against 0.208), whereas resettlement support attenuated it (0.311 against 0.764) (Kim et al., 2026). Coatings should therefore be conditional on tenancy protection and metering regulation, since landlords rather than utilities set subdivided-flat electricity prices, and only 153 prosecutions followed 2,941 overcharging reports (Delina et al., 2026).

Benefits would concentrate among those least able to avoid heat. Of 1,393 older adults in Yau Tsim Mong and Kwun Tong, 60 per cent screened frail; frailty was associated with more heat symptoms (RR 1.28), and living alone protected robust but not frail participants, whose reduced capacity to leave a hot dwelling compounds exposure (Lai et al., 2025). Cooling centres are inadequate: 19 shelters over 70 days averaged nine registered users nightly, which the Government treats as sufficient (Legislative Council, 2025), while 85.7 per cent of industrial-building subdivided-flat residents reported heatstroke symptoms (CarbonCare InnoLab & Kwai Chung Subdivided Flat Community Association, 2024).

Two actions remain available. Residents may locate their building on the district heat-risk map and request coating from the relevant District Council; they may also inform older tenants of the CLP Inverter Air Conditioner Replacement Subsidy, $5 million for approximately 1,200 households, noting that only 36.3 per cent know such support exists (Delina et al., 2026; Legislative Council, 2025).

Indoor heat in subdivided housing is a product of building fabric, not climate alone. Reflective coatings convert an unaffordable cooling problem into a capital works programme; until applied at scale, 220,000 residents will inhabit temperatures the rest of the city does not endure.

portfolios.title: Final Essay

essay.text:
When the thermometer hit 36.9°C at 3 p.m., an old construction worker was still working in construction site under the blazing sun at the brink of heatstroke. When the clock hits 6 p.m., he can finally return to his subdivided flat, hoping for a respite of heat. Lamentably, the ‘cooling’ never came to his rooftop as the entire night stayed at 30.2°C. 

   Due to outer subsiding air of typhoon Dolphin and El Niño effect, the Hong Kong Observatory recorded 36.8 °C on 9 August 2026, the highest recorded temperature since 1884, and it once reached record-breaking high 39.8°C in Sheung Shui(HKO, 2026). However, the Labour Department still remained the lowest level of heat stress at work warning(HSWW), sparking a huge debate that further unveils heat injustice(Lam, 2026).  A study conducted by CarbonCare InnoLab revealed that maximum indoor apparnet temperature in subdivided unit once hit 52.21°C and remained above 50°C at night in summer(CCLI & CSUA, 2026).  The poor are living in a steaming oven: children cannot sleep peacefully while the parents can only use a struggling fan to cool him down and desperately waiting for a cool breeze that will never come. What makes he heat injustice worse is that they almost suffer 24/7: 21.4% of the poor take up elementary occupation including construction labour and outdoor cleaner who work under extreme heat and blazing sunlight in daytime(Oxfam Hong Kong, 2024).

Firstly, we must protect them from suffering in daytime by reforming HSWW. Red and black level has never been activated since its introduction(Labour Department, 2023–2026). Although the  threshold is lowered, the root cause of the issue is the formula. The current formula uses Hong Kong Heat index(HKHI) which was designed for general public instead of outdoor workers(Poon, 2026). HKHI only gives 5% weight for solar radiation (Hong Kong Observatory, 2023) but most outdoor suffer the most physically due to exposion to blazing sunlight. We should replace HKHI by Wet Bulb Globe Temperature(WBGT) which gives a higher 20% weight for solar radiation. On-site measuremnet shows that HKHI underestimate heat stress. On 11th August, WBGT reached 34.1 degree at Kai Tak while HKHI remained at 30 degree(InmediaHK, 2026). According to Japan WBGT guideline, 34.1°C already triggers the highest level ‘Danger’ but HSWW still remained at Amber under same conditions(Ministry of the Environment, n.d.). Just like ‘truth and manufactured doubt’ taught in lecture, HKHI lacks scientific basis for outdoor workers. We are no longer living in an era when manufactured doubt can mislead public and delay protection. It’s time to use a globally recognized WBGT. What we need is a system thinking and understand the cascade effect rather than simply lowering threshold which leaves the root cause, a mismatched formula, behind.

Moreover, we need a multi-pronged approach to protect the poor from extreme heat in nightime. We’ve learnt urban heat island effect and the builidng accounts for 90% electricty consumption. We need to prioritize green retrofitting, lowering the indoor temperature and improving HVAC system right now, rather than new development. We can provide cooling coatings for sudivided-unit residents as coating can lower indoor temperature by 3°C(PolyU, 2024) without creating financial burden. Also, we should provide air-con electricity-bill subsidies to subdivide-unit residents but not simply giving away an air-con without subsidies since most residents cannot afford the bills and can only use it shortly(The Standard, 2026). This is a pragmatic and multi-pronged transition that were taught in lectures but not a blunt and flawed policy.

With multi-pronged approach, the outdoor workers, the crying children and the residents can finally get a respite. The cycle of suffering from extreme heat 24/7 is finally broken. Heat injustice is something that everyone should concern and it’s time to act now. You can raise awareness of heat injustice by advocating for a reform of HSWW and urging construction company to safeguard workers from heat stroke with cooling facilities.  Support the organization concering heat injustice, share the issue with other netizens, keep your air-con temperature above 25°C when possible and care about your elderly neighbours and grandparents during hot nights.

Extreme heat will only get worse but heat injustice can be rectified and broken. Heat injustice can affect everyone across social class. In 20st century, human felt comfortable without air-con but now we are at the brink of heatstroke without air-con. In 2100, is air-con enough for us to survive extreme heat? If we don’t act now, the heat will knock on your doors in 2100. Act now or the heat will devour everyone even with air-con.

portfolios.title: Your Feed Fills Landfills

essay.text:
In June 2024, volunteers on the 11th floor of an office tower in Quarry Bay faced a 16-tonne mountain of donated clothes. Some still had their original tags attached and had never been worn (Knott, 2024). Yet this case is not isolated; a Hong Kong survey found that 39% of respondents had discarded clothing after wearing it just once (YouGov, 2017). But why do we buy clothes we barely wear?

Social media is part of the problem. TikTok trends like #TikTokMadeMeBuyIt introduce viewers to new products, while built-in shopping features make it easier than ever to buy them (Johnson, 2026). Research by Mahn et al. (2026) found that inspiration from fashion hauls was a major contributor to purchase intentions, especially impulsive buying. The constant pressure to follow the latest styles fuels overconsumption and increases textile waste. In Hong Kong, around 400 tonnes of textiles were sent to landfills daily in 2024 (Tsang & Ruan, 2026). However, the environmental impact extends beyond waste. Globally, the fashion industry produces 1.2 billion tonnes of CO₂ annually. If current practices persist, emissions are projected to rise by over 50% by 2030 (Johnson, 2026).

My proposed solution is an app called Rewear. It combines three features to help users reconsider unnecessary purchases and restyle clothes they already own. Although recycling can help tackle textile waste, in 2024 less than 1% of global fibre production came from recycled textiles (Tsang & Ruan, 2026), highlighting the limited role of textile recycling. The key is to prevent overconsumption.

Digital Wardrobe

Users upload photos of their clothing and create different combinations directly in the app, allowing them to recreate trending looks using existing clothes. A Hong Kong survey by Redress (2020) found that 41% of respondents owned unworn clothes because they “forgot they have it”. By helping users rediscover and restyle their clothes, the app could reduce unnecessary purchases. Jiang and Macintyre (2025) also suggest that wardrobe-management apps can encourage more sustainable clothing habits.

“Save now, decide later” wishlist

Instead of buying an item immediately, users could save it to the app. After 24 hours, they would receive a notification asking whether they still want or need it. This pause could encourage more thoughtful purchasing decisions, particularly since 46% of respondents in the same survey identified impulse-driven shopping as a reason for owning unworn clothes (Redress, 2020).

Social Platform

Users could share the outfits they created from clothes they already own, using the hashtag #OutfitRepeater. This aims to make rewearing clothes just as exciting and socially visible as showing off new purchases. Instead of going against social media culture,  Rewear uses it to encourage more sustainable behaviour.

Before expanding across Hong Kong, Rewear could be implemented through a pilot scheme at HKU, targeting young consumers who regularly engage with social media. Its effectiveness could be evaluated by tracking how often students recreated outfits without buying anything new, how many saved items were abandoned after 24 hours, and whether their self-reported impulse purchases decreased. However, photographing an entire wardrobe could be time-consuming, potentially discouraging users from engaging with the app. Instead, students could start by uploading only their most frequently worn clothes and gradually add more.

Rewear could benefit consumers by reducing unnecessary spending and helping them make better use of the clothes they already own. However, the biggest potential benefit would be environmental. According to WRAP (2012), extending the active life of clothing by nine months could reduce its carbon, water, and waste footprints by around 20–30%. By encouraging people to wear their clothes longer, Rewear could help reduce demand for new clothing and the waste its production creates. As Professor Christina Wong emphasises, tackling fashion waste requires preventing it at earlier stages rather than only managing it after disposal (Tsang & Ruan, 2026). If adopted by younger consumers, it could also encourage more sustainable consumption in the long term.

You can start right now. Although Rewear is still a proposed app, the next time you see a trending outfit on TikTok, save it instead of buying it immediately, check your wardrobe for similar pieces, and wait 24 hours before deciding whether you really need it.

The 16-tonne mountain of clothes in Quarry Bay shows what can happen when clothing is bought but barely worn. Rather than only dealing with the waste left behind, Rewear aims to tackle the problem at its source: excessive consumption. Technology has made discovering new clothes easier than ever, so why not use it to rediscover what we already own?

portfolios.title: When Colors Disappear: Saving Hong Kong’s Coral Reefs

essay.text:
When Colors Disappear: Saving Hong Kong’s Coral Reefs

What happens when the ocean that once sustained generations becomes a world their children may only know through photographs? Guanzon grew up in a coastal town in the Philippines. He remembers going out with his father on fishing trips: the boat surrounded by schools of fish so rich that the shallow water grew dark. “When I dove in the ocean, it was even more beautiful”, he claimed, full of regret. Beneath the surface were corals stretching across the seabed, screaming in colors. It was an upside-down world of extraordinary beauty. The ocean was far beyond a workplace; it was his friend, childhood, and livelihood. However, when he returned to those same waters years later, there were “almost no fish”, and patches of coral turned ghostly white. The ocean looked dead. The world that bred his childhood was disappearing in front of him.

Although his story comes from the Philippines, the threat is close to home. Hong Kong, especially in the eastern and northeastern waters around Hoi-Ha-Wan and Yan-Chau-Tong, nurtures 84 species of abundant hard corals (AFCD, 2025), and these homes are increasingly threatened by rising sea temperatures. The temperatures cause the once vibrant corals to starve, expel the microscopic algae that provide their energy, turn completely white, and potentially die due to coral bleaching. In 2022, research regarding Hong Kong’s marine heatwaves reported that the proportion of bleached coral cover across nine surveyed sites ranged from 2.4% to an alarming 70.3% (Chung et al., 2024). Such large-scale local coral bleaching was also recorded by AFCD, where 13 sites in its 2024 Reef Check experienced bleaching associated with prolonged elevated sea temperatures (AFCD, 2025a). This crisis extends beyond Hong Kong and coral reefs alone. The United Nations reported in 2021 that approximately 14% of coral was lost between 2009 and 2018, while coral reefs support at least 25% of marine species (UNEP, 2021). Their disappearance marks a threatening reality to marine biodiversity that devastates the ecological balance of coastal waters and local communities. Hong Kong cannot afford delaying this environmental problem.

To tackle this problem, I propose establishing a Hong Kong Coral Resilience Partnership. We should no longer rely on emergency responses only after we observe bleaching. Instead, we should unite the government, universities, and local fishing communities to protect our remaining corals.

This partnership aims to detect damage before it occurs, identify resilient local coral populations, and restore habitats. First, HK should promote stronger scientific monitoring. AFCD, in its 2025 Reef Check program, surveyed 36 sites with more than 1,300 volunteer divers and concluded that a more comprehensive early-warning network should be developed. Monitoring systems, such as underwater temperature sensors and frequent coral-health checks, are necessary to locate vulnerable locations before bleaching. Through these, climate refugia can also be identified, which are areas where more resilient corals experience less heat stress. Scientists can focus on restoring these locations, while more damaged reefs should be restored only where conditions allow recovery. Indeed, at CUHK, researchers have already established deeper-water nurseries to cultivate stresstolerant corals for potential transplantation. Alongside governmental support, these new technologies can empower a sustainable scientific monitoring system to cultivate a more robust coral community.

Second, restoring corals isn’t effective if damage continues. HK should strengthen ecological protection by valuing biodiverse areas, including Hoi-Ha-Wan and Yan-Chau-Tong. The government also plays an irreplaceable role in coral preservation. Governments should reduce polluted runoff and prevent destructive fishing to restrict activities destroying corals, thereby reducing avoidable local pressures. Above all, as an important step in active conservation, local communities mustn’t be left to carry the burden of restoration alone. Fishers should receive paid training and government-supported employment in reef monitoring. Financial support should also be long-term and available if environmental restrictions affect local business income. Protecting the ocean should never mean sacrificing families.

The responsibility lies greatly on us, too. We should choose responsibly sourced seafood, reduce plastic waste, and support local conservation initiatives to help reduce pressure on marine ecosystems through simple actions. We should demand that marine biodiversity receive actual consideration in Hong Kong’s environmental policies. We cannot stop global warming alone, but we can give vulnerable coral communities a better chance of surviving it. In 2025, Coral Beach in Hoi-Ha-Wan reported an 84.7% coral cover (AFCD, 2025b). This reminds us that Hong Kong still has vibrant marine ecosystems to protect.

One day, our children may ask what Hong Kong’s ocean once looked like. We want our answer to not simply be a photograph of what we failed to save.

essay.text:
Cooling Hong Kong in a Warming World In 2024, Agence France-Presse reported 84 year old retired janitor Chun Loi sweating in her windowless, 50 sqft Hong Kong home despite running two fans. Her story shows how difficult escaping the heat can be when someone lives in a small, poorly ventilated flat. As temperatures rise, keeping people safe depends on the homes and neighbourhoods they live in. Climate change is heating our planet, and 2024 was Earth’s hottest year on record according to CNN. Moreover, in dense cities like Hong Kong, urban design amplifies the problem even further. Concrete buildings and roads absorb heat throughout the day and release it at night. Meanwhile, closely packed towers can block cooling breezes, and limited greenery means less shade and cooling through evaporation. Together, these factors create the phenomena known as the urban heat island, where urban areas remain warmer than nearby areas, especially at night. In 2024 alone, the Hong Kong Observatory reported 50 hot nights, where the temperature never dropped below 28 degrees on those nights. Not only does this heat make daily life uncomfortable, it can also threaten people’s health, as they give the body less chance to recover. A 2020 report by CUHK linked hot nights to a 2.4% higher risk of death, and up to 6.7% for five consecutive hot nights. Outdoor workers, older people, those with existing illnesses and residents of poorly ventilated homes are particularly vulnerable as their bodies face greater stress. Here’s the catch: the hotter our cities get, the more electricity we use for air conditioning. When fossil fuels supply that electricity, the resulting emissions contribute to further global warming, creating a vicious cycle of rising heat & cooling demand. Therefore, we need to break this cycle before our cities become even more dangerous to live in. Hong Kong should focus on two connected priorities: making buildings and streets cooler, and reducing emissions from the energy we use. That starts with improving the places where heat already builds up. The government should fund retrofits to older housing, schools, and care homes. External window shades can block sunlight before it heats rooms, while reflective roofs absorb less solar energy. Developers should also demonstrate how new buildings allow airflow and limit overheating before projects receive approval. The same approach should also extend to public spaces. Transport and planning authorities should provide shade at exposed bus stops and along busy walking routes. Medellín, Colombia shows what shading can achieve. It added greenery along 18 roads and 12 waterways & city officials reported temperature reductions of more than 2°C (UNEP, 2019). Hong Kong

could similarly plant suitable trees along existing streets, then measure the cooling effects before expanding. However, even with better urban design, people will still need air conditioning. This brings us to our second goal of reducing emissions from electricity use. The International Energy Agency (2024) reports that highly efficient air conditioning units can use half as much electricity as average models. The government should therefore subsidize replacement of inefficient units for low income households, helping them stay cool while using and spending less on electricity. Where that electricity comes from matters too. The government and power companies should invest more in renewable energy, such as solar & wind, and work more with neighbouring regions to secure more renewable electricity. Regional cooperation is particularly important because Hong Kong’s limited space constrains local generation (Environment Bureau, 2021). Doing so would reduce Hong Kong’s reliance on fossil fuels and lower emissions from air conditioning and other everyday activities, helping Hong Kong meet its energy needs while playing its part in combating global warming.

Striving for change is one thing, but making these improvements brings practical challenges, as they require upfront spending and regular maintenance. Therefore, to manage costs, the government should introduce cooling upgrades gradually and prioritize neighbourhoods most exposed to heat. Residents can support these changes as well through simple everyday choices. Closing blinds before direct sunlight enters can reduce cooling demand, while taking public transport can help cut emissions. Students can also join campus greening projects and reduce wasted electricity by switching off lights and air conditioning when study rooms are no longer in use. For residents like Chun, these improvements could mean a safer home that costs less to keep cool. By creating cooler neighbourhoods and reducing the emissions that drive warming worldwide, Hong Kong can play its part in tackling climate change while protecting people from the heat they already face. portfolios.title: The Power of Small Swaps

essay.text:
In this world, not everyone might have empathy, but I am sure they have sympathy. People might not care about rising sea levels in Tuvalu or shelter damage in Rohingya, Myanmar, but they can be sensitive enough to understand the suffering of innocent animals and children. The central challenge of climate action is not that humanity is heartless; it is that our daily systems hide environmental harm behind convenience and price tags. After a long day of class, I was heading to my dormitory in Hong Kong. The view is fantastic with a dense skyline, busy harbors with green mountain ridges. But climbing up to my dorm the temperature is too high. Since arriving here, the heat has barely relented, leaving me wondering how millions of residents endure it daily. The answer is simple. It's an air conditioning system that we use. Stepping out of the 30 degrees celsius into the freezing blast of a convenience store, it’s hard to remember that keeping this city cool swallows nearly a third of its electricity consumption making it a major indirect driver of CO2 emissions. But do people really know this fact? It’s questionable. On my way back to my dormitory, I decided to buy some meat. The wide variety of meats are available at the store shelves and I just remembered the lesson we just covered in class, 1 kg of the industrial beef needs 60kg of carbon dioxide emission to be produced. Yet I still reached for the regular industrial beef. I am not a vegetarian, and on a student budget, there was no cheaper meat option. The low CO2 alternative carried a price tag I simply could not justify. After that, I went through a Bazaar, where clothes there are so much cheaper than other stores. I checked the prices and materials. No wonder they were so cheap. It was made of Polyester, the cheapest fabric to produce. Factories make polyester from petroleum, and turning crude oil into plastic threads takes huge amounts of energy. In this way, people buy these clothes without knowing it’s cruel impact on the climate. It’s not their fault to look for cheap clothing. I also used to buy clothings made of polyester. But now I understand the better the materials, the longer it lasts. Standing outside my dorm with a bag of high-emission beef beneath the hum of air conditioners, I just realized why so many people fail to take personal responsibility. Even as someone actively studying about climate change, I fell back on habit and convenience because the impact felt abstract and the actions I am taking felt too small to matter. To move people toward genuine accountability, we cannot rely on guilt or demand overnight perfection. Instead, we need a solution rooted in visible impact and achievable small habits. Throughout my life, I observed how we perceived far better immediate feedback and social norms than than distant warnings. We talk about climate change results, but we rarely educate children and elderly about how to reduce carbon footprints. I am sure plenty of children know about global warming but are they familiar with steps they should take to reduce the impact? They better be told that there is more to do beside classifying the trash. When supermarkets display color-coded carbon footprints on food shelves, when apartments and malls show real time carbon emissions, and the clothing tags reveal the fabric emissions, the cost of consumption would become transparent. Additionally the accountability must be paired with realistic independent small actions that anyone can take financially. The steps are now easy: raising the AC by only 2 degrees, swapping the beef with chicken or vegetables once per week or choosing a cloth with good material.

When millions of individuals take small, independent ownership of their daily habits, these small actions now become significant. Not just significant but a powerful social norm. People are likely to mirror the habits of people around them, creating an effect that will attract millions more. Saving the planet doesn’t mean introducing more effective technological power plants. But very small actions that everyone can easily take in their daily lives. Hence we can’t move to Mars in decades, we need to love what we have, the Earth.

portfolios.title: Causes of the Urban Heat Island Effect

essay.text:
In 2024, Pattie, a 55-year-old cleaner in the New Territories, works outdoors for eight hours every day while suffering from the unbearable heat due to the increased duration of summer in Hong Kong. “Sometimes, when it’s too hot, even the taste of water makes me feel nauseous,” Pattie said. (Lam, 2024). The above case is a vivid illustration of how the hot climate in Hong Kong is threatening people's health with inadequate protections. According to the Hong Kong Observatory, the projection of the 20-year average annual number of hot nights, which is directly linked to the heat island effect, increases from 63 nowadays to 117 in 2100 for intermediate emissions of greenhouse gases, not to mention the high and very high emission scenarios. After analyzing the local conditions, the global data should also be reviewed. If all current pledges and long-term targets are achieved, warming would reach 2.1°C by 2100. (Climate Action Tracker, 2026). These two data provide a full picture of the consequences of climate change in 2100. Noting that the microclimate of Hong Kong is influenced by both the heat island effect and climate change, actions must be carried out to ensure the sustainable livability of our city. With climate change being an inevitable issue on our planet, a few solutions will be proposed to alleviate its impacts in Hong Kong. In terms of governmental policy, more urban greening should be conducted to mitigate the heat island effect. In Hong Kong, parks and green roofs were found to play substantial roles in cooling urban heat, resulting in temperature reductions of 4.9°C and 4.9°C, respectively. (The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, 2024). Not only can urban greening enhance the cooling effect through evapotranspiration, but vegetation can also filter out air pollutants to enhance the escape of radiation. As a result, urban greening is an effective measure to create a sustainable city in the future.

However, the feasibility of urban greening highly depends on the structural standards and waterproofing ability of the building. In 2016, a green roof at the top of the Hu Fa Kuang Sports Centre at City U collapsed, with tons of soil and debris rushing into the hall below. With added weight and heavy rainfall being a crux of the incident, this is a walking portrayal of the importance of building structure and waterproofing systems when applying urban greening. Thus, urban greening is inapplicable in old urban areas, but it can be widely practiced during comprehensive redevelopment to mitigate the heat island effect and establish a more comfortable living environment. Apart from urban planning, the healthcare system, which is already under high pressure, must also strengthen its ability to address the increase in the number of heat-related diseases under climate change. The warming climate could increase healthcare demand in the long run. (Lai et al., 2025). With heatstroke, respiratory diseases, and cardiovascular diseases expected to be more common illnesses under global warming, the healthcare system must be equipped with sufficient staff and instruments to deal with these diseases. Last but not least, for education, the syllabus of secondary education should be modified to raise the awareness of teenagers to protect the environment. According to the GEPCC, climate change is taught only as a topic of geography during the F4 to F6 curriculum, which is an elective subject in secondary education in Hong Kong. Consequently, with climate change being an inescapable issue in our society, it should be incorporated as a necessary topic in the curriculum so that all students have a basic understanding of the mechanisms and consequences of climate change. With reference to research done by Pädagogische Hochschule Freiburg University of Education, results revealed a significant medium to large mean effect size for knowledge-related

outcomes for climate change, and a small to medium effect for attitude-related and behaviorrelated outcomes. This study clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of climate change education in shaping the behaviors of our future generation. Considering that long-term mitigation cannot depend only on the government, awareness of climate protection can be entrenched in residents’ minds to alleviate its impacts on our society. To conclude, “I want you to act as if the house is on fire, because it is,” said Greta Thunberg. The evidence provided in the article shows that Hong Kong is already a burning house. In 2100, with the expectation that the consequences of climate change will be intensified, it is necessary for all stakeholders, including the general public and the government, in Hong Kong to cooperate to work out some effective solutions to ensure the long-term sustainable development of our city. portfolios.title: The Water War: Man vs AI?

essay.text:
The Hidden Thirst of AI: Who Pays the Price?

In Mansfield, a small American town, Beverly Morris’s home is 366 metres away from a Meta AI data centre (AIDC). The AI cloud may be invisible, but her bucket is not: After construction began, her well pressure fell and sediment appeared, forcing her to carry water in buckets to flush her toilet (Fleury and Jimenez, 2025).  While Meta disputes a connection, it remains undeniable that AIDCs drive water use. So, who bears the hidden water cost of AI?

The rise of AI may accelerate water inequality. AIDCs directly consumed an estimated 66 billion litres of water in 2023; By 2028, one single hyperscale centre could consume 60–124 billion litres of water annually, which approximately equals the annual water demand for 17 million people (Shehabi et al., 2024). Many AIDCs use evaporative cooling to cool facilities, evaporating around 80% of water used (Friends of the Earth, 2026; Li et al., 2025).  Beyond cooling, electricity generation and chip manufacturing further intensify water demand (Shehabi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). Yet at the same time, around 1.8 billion people like Beverly still lack safe drinking water at their homes. Worse still, in 7 out of 10 such households, it is often women who are forced to carry heavy water buckets (WHO and UNICEF, 2023). This essay does not solely blame AI for all water shortage problems, but rather questions how individuals and companies can promote better water equality when stronger AI demands more water.

Technological advancement can make AI less thirsty. Starting in 2024, Microsoft has adopted a new cooling method that uses direct-to-chip and closed-loop cooling, reducing more than 125 million litres of cooling water annually (Solomon, 2024). This is promising, but it only replaces evaporative cooling, not the whole supply chain. Operators should use recycled or reclaimed water if appropriate, and avoid building water-intensive facilities in drought-prone areas.

Yet, technological advancements aren’t enough– We need your voice and actions.

First, audit your AI water footprint. We are not discouraging you from using AI, but we should use it responsibly: Try to avoid repeated questions and choose simpler tools for simple tasks. Every question you ask consumes about 10-50 ml of water (Li et al., 2025). Use tools like the Omni AI Water Footprint Calculator (https://l1nq.com/spaifuv) to estimate your water and share it with your friends. When we try to make the intangible tangible, awareness of AI-related environmental problems can be raised.

Secondly, instead of just comparing computing power, choose AI tools that bear environmental responsibility. Try to compare the Water Usage Efficiency (WUE) of different AI companies. You can also check Hugging Face’s public AI Energy Score leaderboard and choose the most efficient model that still does the job (Hugging Face, n.d.). One person alone cannot reform an industry, but informed customers can pressure tech giants to adopt the latest technology for better sustainability. In the drought-prone region of Chile, Cerrillos, residents voted against a proposed Google data centre construction in a local referendum, eventually pressuring Google to adopt a less water-intensive cooling system (McGovern and Branford, 2023). In Monterey Park, Los Angeles, residents protested against building a giant data centre in the region, worrying that AIDC will strain the energy grid and water supply. Community pressure has resulted in statutory reforms in California: AB 2619 now requires operators to report projected water use for permits and actual use when renewing licences, while AB 2469 requires drought planning for new or expanded centres (CalMatters, 2026a; Becker, 2026). This proves that market pressure can force AI tech giants to improve water and energy efficiency.

A full tap now does not guarantee an endless one. About 70-80% of Hong Kong(HK)’s fresh water comes from Dongjiang (Water Supplies Department, 2026). We may not face water shortage today, but our water security relies heavily on one shared river and careful planning. HK and China may follow the laws passed in California to require AI companies to disclose their water footprint and bear environmental responsibility. Yet, the whole transformation begins with a little more responsibility, a little more awareness and a little more pressure.

It is not a zero-sum game between water, people and AI development. Use AI responsibly, demand clear water data, and speak up for water-shortage safeguards now. The goal is not to stop the cloud, but to make sure it does not leave someone else’s tap dry. Act now, when the tap still flows. Rethink, to save your tokens, and to save the water.

essay.text:
The Right to Have a Home

I want to start with a number that sounds like a mistake: twelve hundredmillion. By 2050, that is how many people may be displaced by climate change,and over two billion by the end of the century. In 2020, we already had morethan 80 million refugees (UNHCR, n.d.-a). I did not believe it at first. Then I realised I already knew some of these people.

They are the ones I have walked past for three years in Hong Kong. This cityholds one of the highest concentrations of millionaires in the world, and is alsoone of the most unequal places to live: about 1.4 million people live on lessthan HK$4,500 a month, a poverty rate of 21.4%, and roughly 13,000 asylumseekers and refugees survive alongside them in what has been called "theworld's least unaffordable real estate." I had never connected these people tothe climate crisis. I do now.

Because this crisis is not only about water. It is about law.

Here is what shocked me most. There is no such thing as a climate refugee.Under the 1951 Refugee Convention, you qualify only if you have awell-founded fear of persecution (UNHCR, n.d.-c). Rising seas do notpersecute anyone. So a family whose island is disappearing has no legalcategory to stand in. Entire island nations are now

certain to disappear withsea-level rise, and their people would arrive with no status at all (UNHCR,n.d.-a). As McDonnell (2018) reports, these are "the refugees the world barelypays attention to" - displaced by weather, not war, and therefore protectedby no one.

Think about what that actually means. A country with no war, no crime, andalmost no emissions can be sentenced to disappear - not for what it did, butfor what we did. Their people did the least to cause this, and they will be asked to leave first.

We spent the semester learning that climate change is a systems problem. Theweek on energy and transport showed me that our choices about power decidewho breathes clean air. The week on cities and buildings showed me that thebuilt environment decides who survives a heatwave. The week on capital andthe commons showed me that money flows towards whoever already haspower. By the time I reached the week on displacement, the pattern wasimpossible to miss: climate change does not create new injustice. It pours itselfinto the injustice that already exists.

That is why I am not proposing another technology. I am proposing a definition.

My solution is to build legal recognition for climate-displaced people - a protection status that does not require proof of persecution. It would beginwith regional

agreements: Pacific island states and their larger neighbourssigning binding commitments to accept people displaced by sea-level rise, withrights to work, housing and long-term support rather than temporary visas. Itwould mean governments formally recognising that sovereignty can continueeven when land does not. And it would give citizens of disappearing islandssomething they currently lack: a legal plan for the day the water arrives. Why this and not something else? Because the money alone is not arriving.The UN Environment Programme's Adaptation Gap Report 2025 finds thatdeveloping countries will need roughly $310 billion per year by 2035 forclimate adaptation, while international public adaptation finance stood at only$26 billion in 2023 - a gap of twelve to fourteen times (UNEP, 2025). A gapthat size is not solved by goodwill. It is solved by rules that decide who is owedprotection, and who pays for it. This matters in Hong Kong too, because a citythat already hosts 13,000 people in legal limbo has the institutions to helpdefine what comes next.

I know what the objection is. The numbers are contested, the scale isoverwhelming, and opening a new legal category could be slow, expensive andpolitically toxic. I take that seriously. But the alternative is what we have now:silence. A definition that does not exist protects no one. And the objection that'we cannot help everyone" has never been a reason to help no one.

So this is what I would ask you to do. When climate displacement appears inyour news feed, do not scroll past the word "refugee" as if it were settled. Askinstead: under what law? If your answer is "none," then you have found thegap I am talking about. Push the institution you belong to -a university, acompany, a city - to formally recognise climate displacement. Support thecampaigns, and vote for the people who will write the definition.

Because the sea is rising whether or not we have a word for it. And a personwho loses a country should not also lose the right to be recognised.

Environmental Education--Is it right?

I have been educated as an environmentally conscious person ever since I was in primary school. Ten years pass, I can still recall the mast landfill pictures that our teacher shown in order to brief us on how the impacts of climate change is growing. Having a deep impression on this, I have tried my best to replicate the instructions given by our teacher and mainstreamed media to fight against the worsen of the climate situations. Simple habits like using canvas or cotton bangs instead of plastic ones and use vacuum cup to avoid the consumption of deposit one have ingrained into my life. I have to admit that I am proud of my participation and sincerely hope that more people can take action and join the campaign.

This September, I walked into the classroom and learned a boarder picture of climate change. The professor elaborated on the more aspects that may cause climate change, from food consumption to energy transport. “The food consumption concealed a deeper problem that is beyond our impression.” As the professor’s speaking, I recognized that the link between food consumption and the intensification of climate change is tight. For example, Hong Kong import 90% of the food, the pollution emitted during food consumption, the Carbon Dioxide and the Nitric oxide etc., should undoubtedly claim for climate change. Apart from this, the heat island effect generating by the urbanization, the tons of dye water in fast fashion industry, the dominance of traditional method of power generation....My perspective of climate change gradually change. It is not just about simple plastic bags and disposable bottles, every shirt I wear, every piece of food in my stomach, every bus ride....Human life itself seems to be the “culprit” of climate change.

After class, I walked into a restaurant for lunch. Staring at the steak on my plate, the professor’s voice was still resounding. “How much carbon dioxide will be given out in just this meal?”, “why did I didn’t realize that simply eating, is worsening the situation of climate change?”, “Did anyone remind me before?”... The education that I received in the early age never stress the ubiquity of the factor that intensity climate change. Therefore, only now do I realize how pervasive climate change has become, already permeated into our life, which is a wide-ranging and urgent issue that we cannot tackle only by controlling the use of plastic product. But most of the kids received the same education, holding an incomplete and shallow perspective to climate change, forming awareness that is inaccurate.

Therefore, regarding this topic, I cannot help but question the effectiveness of the environmental education I received throughout my compulsory school years. Starting from scratch to let students form the habit of bringing own bags and bottles are undoubtedly worthwhile, but these habit only present the tip of iceberg. The education system presents climate as a problem that can be solved through individual and surface-level actions, but ignore that the problem itself is driven by systematic factors, and the deeper solution is absent from the curriculum. This education created a false sense of security: when I am not carrying plastic bags or using disposable bottle, I am doing my part. But the truth is, the students do not understand the complexity of the issue, and their effort is like clearing the ocean with a spoon.

This realization leads me to a clear conclusion, which is also the answer the question of how to move people, especially children to take action: government and educational institutions must expand and deepen the education on climate change. It should stop only teaching children how to do simple things like turning off the light and saving water as well as the reducing the use of plastic products. It must involve a comprehensive curriculum that explain the inner connection between the human activity and climate change. Through tracing a cotton shirt from farm to factory to home and calculating the carbon cost of a steak, the children will realize that “we should do more to protect the environment.

Some may think that this will let more people to support the climate instead of the development. But environmental education should not be confined to science or geography, it is a common topic for economics and sociology. Through which, they will expose to a boarder notion, examing whether people should support development or climate in different issue, helping them to develop the literacy to clarify their own stance. Through the cross-disciplinary involvement can help students build up their own viewpoint, enabling them to take wise action when facing climate-change related problem in the future.

To conclude, this course has given me inspiration on the deficiency of the whole picture in the environmental education. It is urgent that government and related institution revising the syllabus and build up children’s discernment.

essay.text:
Reconnect with your closet - end fast fashion from within!

I own almost 200 items of clothing. Over the last month I wore roughly 40 of them (if I’m being generous). As I cleaned out my closet, I uncovered over 50 pieces of clothing that I hadn’t touched in months, and five I couldn’t remember having worn at all. One was a crimson skirt stuffed in the back of my closet, tag still on, in a color I didn’t even know I owned. Had I become so caught up in following trends that I stopped paying attention to what I buy?

Standing in front of my closet, I wondered how different things could have been if I simply noticed the skirt and wore it more. WRAP, a UK-based charity, found that extending the active life of a piece of UK clothing by 9 months could reduce carbon, waste and water footprints by up to 20% (Let’s recycle, 2017). In less than a year, I could’ve actually created a positive impact, but instead I kept shopping. I realise now that the problem wasn't that I had nothing to wear, it was that I wasn't wearing what I already had.

One article argued that fast fashion thrives on a constant influx of new stock that creates a sense of exclusivity, pushing people to buy things they don’t need. Mango, for example, has been releasing new products every two weeks since February 2016 (Sustainable brands, 2018). Reading this made me realise that somewhere between the sales and new arrivals, I had stopped asking myself if I needed any of it. To me, this felt connected back to what we learned in class about incentives; people don’t act in a vacuum, they respond to the system around them. I didn’t buy the skirt because I’m careless, I bought it because I saw a good deal.

This isn’t isolated to just my closet. In Hong Kong, a 2017 independent survey discovered that out of 1000 local residents, 4 in 10 people discarded clothing after only wearing it once (South China Morning Post, 2018). Read that again, once. Hong Kong alone sent an average of 388 tonnes of textiles to the city’s overflowing landfills every day and about half of that was estimated to be clothing (South China Morning Post, 2018). Behind each of these tonnes is the energy and water it took to make the clothes in the first place, only for them to be worn briefly and be discarded (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2017).

In Hong Kong, second-hand clothing has recently gained traction amongst younger people. Students are ditching malls for small second-hand stores in places like Mong Kok searching for hidden treasures they consider to be retro and vintage (Shroffed, 2026). However, a psychological barrier remains with one HKU student stating she preferred new clothes because they feel “cleaner and more comfortable” (Lifestyle.inq, 2018). In today’s fast-fashion age, our brains have been trained to see new as better and old as lesser.

The solution I want to focus on is simple: it is to keep clothes in use for longer by creating a culture of swapping and exchanging. Rather than waiting for the fashion industry giants to change their ways, we can work to build a more circular economy ourselves (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2017). Take out plastic’s (a local charity) TOP Swop events let people exchange clothing in a collective, shared space and so reduce the sense of taboo associated with secondhand clothing.

Yes, swapping does mean giving up the thrill of buying something new, but at the same time hunting for a hidden find on a swap table can be just as fun, and nobody has to pay for it, not even the environment! Even though swaps can’t fix the whole system, they can help to keep clothes in use longer, which ties back to WRAP’s research points (Let’s Recycle, 2017). There’s no need for some big authority or council to get involved. Just ask ten friends to bring three items that they no longer find themselves wearing, and bring a needle and thread for the rest.

Sifting through my closet showed me that the problem wasn’t that I needed more space but rather that I needed to value what I already owned. The crimson skirt is still at the back, and I’m not throwing it away. Instead, I’m going to take it with me to my first swap, and I hope someone finally wears it.

Count the Wears Before You Buy

essay.text:
Every girl I know has stood in front of a packed wardrobe an hour before a dinner and said the same sentence: "I have nothing to wear." I say it before nearly every business event, even though my clothes fill wardrobes both at home and in my HKU dorm. Last time, the only bottoms that went with my new top were in the wash, so I seriously considered buying an identical pair, and I ended up in the same outfit I always wear. Somewhere along the way it stopped feeling like a fashion emergency and started to feel like a habit I could not break. My problem is a small version of a large one. Hong Kong disposes 404 tonnes of textiles on average per day, and the quantity of textiles accounted for less than 1% of the quantity of recyclables recovered from municipal solid waste. (Environmental Protection Department, 2021). Globally, while productions of textiles doubled from 2000 to 2015, the duration of a garment being worn has fallen by 36% (Environment Programme, 2025). None of this crossed my mind while I stood in front of my wardrobe, and the real issue is not how many clothes we own, but how few times we wear each one. The solution I propose is a simple rule: count the wears before you buy. If you will wear something only once, rent or borrow it nearby, and if you will wear it again and again, buy one good piece and keep wearing it. This follows the lesson of the cotton tote bag from our course, which only becomes better than a plastic bag after at least 131 uses (CCGL9065, Lecture 3), because whether a choice is green depends on how often the item is used. The mechanism is direct: the impact of making a garment is fixed, so every extra wear spreads it thinner, and Johnson & Plepys (2021) found that renting formal dresses increased the number of times each dress was used and reduced its impact over its whole life. WRAP (2017) similarly found that extending the use of existing garments reduces production and processing impacts, provided that it replaces the purchase of new clothes.

The strongest objection is that rental is not automatically green, and this is correct. The Guardian (2021) found, in a study of jeans, that wearing clothes longer gives the lowest climate impact and that rental can have the highest if it makes people travel more, while Johnson and Plepys (2021) similarly found that the benefit depends on how often garments are worn, whether rental replaces buying, and how customers travel to the rental store. My own rental passed that test, since my prom dress cost HK$580 with accessories included and came from a shop only two MTR stops from my home, which I collected on the day and returned the next, whereas buying a similar dress would have cost between HK$1,000 and HK$9,000 for a single evening. Implementation needs two shifts. First, individuals can apply the rule themselves, and for business events that recur I would rather buy a dress I can wear repeatedly. Second, institutions can make the sensible choice the easy one, for example by having student societies and faculties keep a shared rack of formal wear on campus, so that borrowing needs no courier and no extra journey. The people who benefit first are those building a work wardrobe, who must look professional at many events, often on a limited budget, and this rule allows both. The environment benefits too, because every extra wear means one fewer new garment needs to be produced, and the rule removes a social worry as well, since repeating a dress chosen deliberately is a decision. Before your next event, write down how many times you expect to wear the outfit: if the answer is once, rent or borrow it from a shop near you, and if the answer is many, buy one piece that goes with at least three things you already own. My top that matched only one pair of bottoms would have failed that test. My wardrobe was full and I still had nothing to wear, because the problem was never how much I owned but how rarely I wore each piece. Count the wears before you buy, and you will spend less, look just as sharp, and leave less behind.

essay.text:
Blue Economy and Marine Ecosystem: From Exploitation to Protection

Mr. Wong has worked in fishery for decades. He reads the sea like his old friend, knowing every wave and tide. But on one day, when he picked up his nets, his hands froze. There were fewer and stunted fish, with single-use plastics and industrial pollutants. He felt like the tide turned against everything he knew.

Mr. Wong’s empty net is not an isolated misfortune. This mirrors a global pattern. Marine ecosystems are facing severe threats from climate change. Ocean warming destroys stability of capture fisheries. Global production of tuna and swordfish is estimated to decrease by 36%, with fish size reduction by 15% by 2050 (ErauskinExtramiana et al., 2023). These declines illustrate the significance of mitigating climate change to sustain and meet market demand.

Hong Kong’s water also tells the same story. The fishing industry in Hong Kong yielded around 90460 tonnes of fishery produce by over 10000 local fishermen in 2025, offering stable marine supply to consumers (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation

Department, 2026), illustrating the need for supporting local fisheries to promote food and job security.

For traditional fishers like Mr. Wong, who rely on ocean to make a living, the deteriorating marine ecosystem should be addressed with proactive marine protection to save coastal communities, fishing industry and the ocean. Therefore, I propose a 3step strategy of community-led marine protected areas (MPAs) that protect, clean and shield the waters.

The first step is expanding MPAs beyond current coverage. Hong Kong’s marine protected coverage has risen from 2% to 6% (WWF Hong Kong, 2026) but is far from the target of 20% in the government’s Five-Year Plan (HKSAR, 2026), showing insufficient protection of marine environment. Evidence shows why small area is not enough. Using Philippines as an example, after MPA implementation on Balicasag, Balicasag sanctuary increased living hard coral cover by 119% from 1984 to 1999 (Christie et al., 2002), showing higher biodiversity and improved marine environment. However, when the committee was replaced by tourism authority, fish stocks dropped. Therefore, Hong Kong government should establish community-led MPAs with a co-

management model. The Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department could collaborate with fishers to manage MPA. Fishers could become guardians of the fisheries and protect the fisheries they depend on.

The second step focuses on stricter waste regulations. Zhang et al. (2026) conducted a study and found that small microplastics in Hong Kong coastal waters are at average concentration of 362 particles/m³, which is 100 times higher than large microplastics collected. The most abundant polymer is polyethylene terephthalate from machinewashed materials. Protection means little when pollution continues. Thus, Hong Kong should implement stricter waste controls, including making microplastic filters in commercial laundry and municipal wastewater plants mandatory and phasing out single-use plastics. Hence, microplastics are kept out of water, protecting not only marine species but also consumers who eat seafood.

The third step is coastal habitat restoration. Healthy coral reefs reduce wave energy by 97% (Ferrario et al., 2014) but the bleached and degraded ones lose this function. Consequently, Hong Kong’s marine resilience is lowered, more prone to extreme weather events. This city has demonstrated the success of restoration. In Tolo Harbour,

1000 coral fragments are transplanted, achieving 85% survival rate. In Hoi Ha Wan, 3D-printed reef tiles provide habitat for marine species. Mangroves in Mai Po likely protected Fairview Park from flooding during super-typhoon Mangkhut. As a result, Hong Kong should expand mangrove, coral and seagrass restoration to rebuild wavedissipation capacity that warming has destroyed. Hence, coastal and marine environment could be better protected.

This comprehensive solution benefits diverse stakeholders. Indeed, mrarine environment is protected from external human damage. By expanding co-managed MPAs, fishers could be financially stable with protected fish stocks. Families living in coastal area would be less prone to severe weather events under wave-dissipation by species. With waste regulations, seafood consumers could eat safer foods without microplastics. Lastly, the next generation who inherits current marine environment would be protected.

Readers can show support by avoiding seafood listed on IUCN Red List, asking restaurants where their stocks come from, and expressing opinion on adopting sustainable purchasing. Every meal affects the ocean future, and you can make the

choice.

The tide that turned against Mr. Wong’s thinking was not only owing to nature. It was also traceable to human choices. But we can turn it back by choosing differently. MPA is not a fence but a promise that fish we take today will still be there tomorrow.

essay.text:
Cheap Clothes, Expensive Wreckage: How Fast Fashion Exploits the Planet

Buying a 50 HKD item on Shein or Taobao feels like a steal, and the wardrobe is quickly piled with cheap clothes of poor quality, all for less than $100. The next day, those clothes are thrown away after one wear because they are either not for daily occasions or lose shape after just one wash. Somewhere far away, where cotton is grown, the environment is destroyed without us being aware.

The processes of producing textiles are famously costing us too much. Cotton, for instance, is the most common and accounts for over 80% of natural fiber use (Şener Fidan et al., 2023) and created a fashion empire with its softness. According to Chapagain et al. (2006), one T-shirt is estimated to need 2700 liters of water, and the UN (2022) reported that the fashion industry generates 2- 8% of global greenhouse gas emissions while using millions of Olympic-sized swimming pools' worth of water every year. Not only cotton, all natural fiber production also requires a surprisingly huge amount of water, takes up land for animals and trees, and causes soil degradation, not to mention the pesticides and fertilization used. And although overconsumption of clothes is in the global north, it is the producing countries, mostly the global south, that bear the consequences of degrading land and factory emissions. Synthetic fiber, on the other hand, is nothing better: produced from fossil fuels, the

carbon footprint of a ton of polyester is approximately 21,000 kgCO2e in the UK (Thomas et al., 2012), and they release tens of thousands of microfibers with every wash, resulting in an estimated 51 trillion microplastic particles in the ocean (UN, 2024). Even worse, the “crazy” fashion industry is not only linked to environmental destruction but is also well-known for human rights issues.

Fast fashion giant Shein has always been known for cheap clothing and rapid growth but is always mentioned when fast fashion emission problems and inhumane treatment issues emerge. Shein reported a CO2 emission in 2023 that was almost double that in 2022, and this is partly caused by the enormous scale of the business: at any time, 600,000 items are on sale. The overproduction is not an accident, but a systematic issue tightly linked with the natural desire of humans and the economic incentive of generating profit. Shein was reported to have profits of 2 billion (BBC News, 2024) while producing 1,228,000 metric tons of waste in 2026 (Winther, 2026). Yet, when facing criticisms, the company often refuses to answer or distracts the public (Mulkey, 2024).

Hong Kong is deeply entangled in this global system as we import massive quantities of fast fashion. Gen Z-favorite brands like Brandy Melville, Cotton On, H&M, Zara, and all the e-commerce platforms are part of the fast fashion overconsumption system. Around 400 tons of clothes are discarded daily in Hong

Kong (Redress, 2025), and this number piles up to more than 110,000 tons per year, which is 1,400 T-shirts per minute and could cover 25,000 Hong Kong Stadiums, according to Greenpeace (2015). Meanwhile, the same synthetic fabrics we wear shed microplastics into our coastal waters every time we wash them. We are all in the system of creating climate damage for everyone to pay.

Although promotion against overconsumption solves some of the issue, it is inappropriate to blame only the individuals; systematic accountability is also required. The Hong Kong government can impost a mandatory extended producer responsibility scheme on fashion retailers, which makes brands pay for the production costs and fund textile sorting and recycling infrastructure. Critics may argue that this will raise clothing prices for low-income families. However, the current pricing is only an illusion risking the global environment. We are already paying for fast fashion through the public cost of waste management and the health impacts of microplastics. Clothing manufacturing factories and brands are producing easily broken clothes faster than consumers could buy, and doesn’t throwing clothes away after only one wear create even more costs than buying something that lasts long? By making brands absorb the true cost, we force them to design durable, circular clothing.

In conclusion, the bargain of a $50 shirt is not what it seems, the lowered price is paid by both exploited workers and the environment, with the cost bared by the global

south. Although a scheme may ask brands to take some of the responsibilities, we as individuals should also review our consuming habits and make efforts in changing the way the world shops.

essay.text:
The Cloud Has a ground floor Imagine if you could ask an artificial intelligence tool to create a picture of a greener tomorrow. Instantly, a city is drawn up on the screen. It has trees along the streets, with clean waters running through the foundations of buildings. I can still see the creation of this image, but I cannot see what was used to make it. In my work, titled "The Cloud Has a Ground Floor", I added a staircase at the chat window so viewers could follow the process behind the picture. From Hong Kong, I am able to submit a request but I do not know where the processing will occur. So the answer will appear here but the power and cooling will be supplied somewhere else. According to the International Energy Agency (2025), data centers accounted for about 1.5% of global electricity in 2024. This number includes all data centers, including those used for purposes other than artificial intelligence, but it helps me to I know more about the general scale, but I still have the question: what is the resource that the AI service I use depend on? During the discussions of artificial intelligence and climate change in Week 1, I could visualize electricity. Meanwhile, during Week 4, I reflected on where that electricity comes from, as knowing the source will make a difference in the emissions. The life cycle perspective that we discussed in Week 3 helped broadened the understanding of this issue. For instance, the manufacture process of chip could release harmful greenhouse gases (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2026). While replacing AI hardware can also add to electronic waste (Wang et al.,2024) The illustration in my poster indicates another angle of the discussion: some data centers use water for cooling, and generating electricity can also consume water (Shehabi et al., 2024). Thanks to the discussions that we had in Week 10, I can understand further the significance of the blue pipe, power meter, and discarded circuit boards being represented on the same picture. I see the staircase in a more practical sense. AI providers can offer a hyperlink stating "Environmental Information" next to the chat screen. By opening this hyperlink, people can be able to see where the electricity is coming from, the level of greenhouse gases provided by the provider, the quantity of consumed water, and the e-waste. Each one of these points can be addressed separately. For example, a person living near a data center can see directly what is being done with the water in the area. Providers should start with their annual measurements that they can reliably report on for their facilities. The annual report would provide data on the year, location, unit, and what data was captured on the given provider. When a number is reflective of the entire organization in its entirety, then that should be noted. If there is no solid number available from the provider for a specific type of service, then that number should state “not disclosed.” The provider should note how that estimation was made and what the gray areas of uncertainty are. This

would provide an avenue for providers to post pertinent data without claiming that they can measure the effects of all requests placed. The panel can also include the reduction goals beside the actual data. An independent reviewer can verify if the information being presented reflects actual change or just another form of measurement. Users can compare the services when providers measure and report the figure with the same scale. The immediate step that an individual can be taken is to go to the environmental report for the AI service they are using. Select a question such as the source of the electricity. Find out if the answer is only in regards to that specific service or whether the entire company is being referenced. If the information is not clear, then contact the provider for clarity. Even with this visual representation of creating greener cities through AI, I still remain excited about asking AI to draw cleaner cities. This staircase calls upon viewers to stop and think for a moment about the places and resources that made the image possible.
