essay.text:
-Tracing the journey of Trashion: Our Trends, Their TrashLast winter, I cleared out the old clothes in my wardrobe without hesitation, assuming they do not matter to me anymore. But what I did not acknowledge is that they just vanished from a Hong Kong closet only to reappear in a landfill—never really disappearing in this world. In Ghana, around 15 million second-hand garments (Gelbart, 2025) from all around the globe arrive every week. These garments find a second life by being resold and remade at the Kantamanto Market. It sounds like a fairytale, but not all garments share the same future. Damaged garments and torn fibres often end up as waste sitting on beaches or rotting on the bottom of lagoons, leaving local communities bothered. Decluttering frees the wardrobe–yet it fills up distant landfills. Clothes could be buried, but their true cost can never be hidden. Apparently, responsibility is the only thing not included in the receipt. The consequence is clear: cheap clothing does not eliminate costs, it just induces new ones and imposes them on the environment and garment workers. In Hong Kong, an average of 402 tonnes of textiles (Redress, 2025) entered landfills daily in 2023. Natural fibres in landfills release methane as they decompose, trapping heat in the atmosphere. However, the environmental cost does not end when clothes enter a landfill. Clothing wastes also contribute to marine pollution, killing off sea animals. According to HK01, a beaked whale died stranded at Tai O, with canvas bags in its digestive system. The incident reflects a wider problem: our culture of fast fashion and impulsive consumption leaves an everlasting burden on innocent marine life. It is an instant gratification for us, but a lasting cost for the ecosystem. Learning how our impulsive shopping harms the environment calls for immediate action. In terms of legislation, the Hong Kong Government could introduce extended producer responsibility for textile wastes. In 2007, France made an effort by introducing a textile responsibility system for recycling footwear and textiles. (ADEME, n.d.) Through Refashion, various clothing companies are motivated by financial incentives to help collect, sort, repair and recycle unwanted clothes. Brands are also rewarded for extending the lives of clothes, encouraging them to support upcycling. Specifically, Hong Kong could learn from France’s “eco-modulation” fee model, helping to collect funds for subsidizing sorting facilities. This in turn promotes sustainable fashion. As for producers and consumers, they could build a more circular fashion. According to the WTO, circular fashion helps change the habit of buying and discarding by introducing alternatives. Brands contribute by making clothes that last longer and are easy to repair, while consumers could make an effort by swapping clothes or buying second hand ones. When old garments are no longer wearable, the materials could be recycled and made into new clothes, giving them a second life. Ultimately, the amount of textiles being sent to the landfill decreases and reduces the need for new materials. The aim is not to discard the clothes elsewhere, but to stop their toxic cycle of becoming waste. These actions could promote sustainable fashion across Hong Kong. Second hand clothes, swapping and repairing give citizens an alternative to buying new ones, encouraging them to cherish what they have. They can begin with one practical step: starting a one month no new clothes trend, or trading clothes at local stores like Green Ladies. With adequate promotion in learning about consequences brought by fast fashion, citizens would be motivated to change their habits in hopes of safeguarding

the future of the oceans and the environment. It allows them to gain more control over their wardrobe choices, making fashion more ethical and sustainable. Sustainable fashion promotes a stronger implication: It changes our values towards what we consider as a fair price for clothing. Clothes are not truly cheap if someone has to deal with the wastes and aftermath. Brands should not be indifferent once sales have been made and damage has been caused. Upcycling clothes makes us reflect on our attitude towards "Conspicuous consumption”. It encourages us to value what we already own, rather than constantly looking for replacements to fulfill our gratification. The excitement of a new outfit should not come at the expense of our future far from the checkout counter. Our goal is not simply to keep clothes out of landfills, but stop inflicting the consequences that were made for fulfilling our desires onto innocent people and animals. Let “Our Trends, Their Trash” be a slogan in the past–let’s change what we buy and what we keep to secure a bright future for all. essay.text:
Inside the library of The University of Hong Kong (HKU), it is easy to find students wearing hoodies or jackets even in the summer. In contrast, a subdivided flat in Kwun Tong with no air conditioner reached 39°C in July 2025 (Hong Kong Free Press, 2025). Paradoxically, people in Hong Kong are too cold and too hot in the same city. In Hong Kong, buildings use about 90 percent of the city’s electricity (HKSAR Government, 2024), and most of this electricity is produced by burning natural gas and coal (HKSAR Government, 2026). The average temperature has been rising for decades due to human activities that release tons of carbon emissions. The temperature rise not only creates higher demand for air conditioners but also requires enormous amounts of fuel for energy production. This trend is likely to continue, and the energy demand from air conditioners worldwide is expected to triple by 2050 (International Energy Agency, 2018). In 2012, the Hong Kong government launched the Energy Saving Charter, which asks buildings to keep the indoor temperature between 24°C and 26°C in summer. In 2026, more than 3,500 premises, including 247 shopping centers, signed it (Earth.Org, 2026). However, malls have the freedom not to follow the pledge. In a 2016 survey, nine out of ten malls that signed the Charter kept their indoor temperature outside the range (Earth.Org, 2026). Since keeping customers is far more important than saving energy for shopping centers (Kwok et al., 2017), they have little reason to follow the commitment. For this reason, it is essential to set a legal limit on the lowest indoor temperature in large commercial buildings. In South Korea, for instance, public institutions are legally required to keep the indoor temperature at 28°C or above in summer (Jun et al., 2020). Compared to South Korea, a 24°C limit would be quite a generous policy that would not face a fierce backlash from the public. Only a simple amendment to the existing building energy law would be needed to make this policy real.

The new rule should start with the buildings that have already agreed to the Charter. Inspections would be held regularly, especially during the summer. If a building breaks the rule, it would be charged a penalty, and the money could be used for the public good, such as helping low-income families pay their summer electricity bills. According to CLP Power, raising the temperature by 1°C reduces electricity use by 3 percent (Earth.Org, 2026). Mall operators may argue that shoppers like it cold. Kwok et al. (2017) studied shopping malls in Hong Kong and found that most visitors were satisfied with the temperature, and that the malls were not as cold as people believed. However, the same study found that the voluntary agreement on temperature was working poorly. Moreover, 24°C is the lowest point of the 24 - 26°C range that the government itself recommends, so a law would not ask for anything new. And if every mall follow the same rule, no mall would lose customers to a colder one. Consequently, this policy would benefit three different groups. First, building owners would pay lower electricity bills. Second, with less electricity use, the city would release less carbon and less waste heat, which eases the urban heat island effect. Lastly, low-income residents could get support for their cooling costs, which improves their quality of living. Without this policy, those who are financially stable would keep overcooling their rooms, while those with limited financial means would keep suffering from the heat. There is something readers can do today. Set your own air conditioner to 25°C. Also, when a mall or a classroom feels too cold, send one email to the Environment and Ecology Bureau and ask them to make the 24°C minimum mandatory. Students in the HKU library should not need hoodies in summer, and a family in Kwun Tong should not have to sleep in a 39°C room. Hong Kong already has enough cooling. It just needs a rule to share it fairly.

portfolios.title: Beyond Technology: The Role of Communication and Community Engagement in Climate Action

essay.text:
Beyond Technology: The Role of Communication and Community Engagement in Climate Action Climate change is one of the most pressing challenges facing society today, affecting not only the environment but also economic systems, public health, and social equity. Through this course, I realised that climate change is far more complex than I initially assumed. By reflecting on the themes of consumption, systems thinking, and public engagement, I argue that the solution with the greatest potential to promote climate awareness and meaningful impact is not a single technology or policy, but storytelling, communication, and community engagement that can change people's attitudes and behaviours towards sustainability. Before this course, I believed climate change was primarily a technological problem. I assumed that advances in renewable energy, carbon capture, and sustainable materials would be sufficient to drive society towards sustainability. However, the lectures on democracy, capitalism, and climate change challenged this assumption. A particularly influential example was the lecture on consumption and fashion. While solutions such as reducing emissions and encouraging recycling appeared straightforward, the lecture highlighted barriers including product traceability, environmental monitoring, and limited recycling infrastructure. These examples revealed the complexity of implementing sustainable policies. More importantly, the lecture encouraged me to focus on the causes of waste rather than its management. The discussion of fast fashion showed how consumer culture drives excessive production and disposal of clothing. I was surprised to learn that Hong Kong sends more than 400 tonnes of textile waste to landfills every day. This prompted me to question whether technology and regulations alone can solve climate change. I realised that even environmentally friendly products would have limited impact if overconsumption remains unchanged. Climate change is therefore not only a technological challenge but also a cultural one that requires changes in attitudes and consumption habits. Another important lesson from the course was understanding climate change through a systems-thinking perspective. Before taking this course, I often viewed environmental issues as separate problems that could be solved individually. However, the lectures on food systems and green retrofitting demonstrated how climate change is interconnected with social, economic, and cultural systems. The food systems lecture showed that food-related emissions involve more than dietary choices. Food production is linked to land use, water consumption, transportation, global supply chains, affordability, and cultural preferences. Likewise, green retrofitting is affected by implementation costs, ownership issues, public acceptance, and long-term maintenance. These examples showed that climate change cannot be solved through isolated actions because environmental outcomes are interconnected. This reflects systems-thinking principles, which emphasise understanding environmental problems through their social, economic, and ecological relationships (Vallet et al., 2023). One of the most valuable lessons I learnt from this course was the importance of storytelling in driving climate action. During the first lecture, I was introduced to the idea that a

compelling story must be relevant to its audience. Reflecting on my own experience, I realised that climate change initially felt distant and abstract, often presented through scientific terminology and statistics disconnected from daily life. However, I gradually understood that effective climate action depends on making environmental issues personally meaningful. This view is supported by Moser and Dilling (2007), who argue that climate communication, public outreach, and education are essential for encouraging behavioural change and collective action. Communication and public engagement can make complex concepts tangible. Clothing swap events, community gardens, beach clean-ups, and tours of retrofitted green buildings can help people connect environmental issues to their daily lives. These examples showed me that facts alone are often insufficient to motivate behavioural change. People engage more readily with climate issues when they can experience and relate to them. Therefore, I believe that storytelling, communication, and community engagement have the greatest potential to create climate awareness and inspire collective action. Ultimately, this course transformed my understanding of climate change. I moved from viewing it as a technological problem to recognising it as a complex issue shaped by culture, economics, and interconnected systems. While technology and policies remain important, I now believe that storytelling, communication, and community engagement have the greatest potential to create lasting impact. By making environmental issues personally relevant, these approaches can encourage behavioural change and inspire collective action towards a more sustainable future.

Break The Heat Cycle: Rethinking Hong Kong’s Dependence on Air-Conditioning

On a hot summer afternoon in Hong Kong, stepping into an air-conditioned shopping mall or office feels like immediate relief. However, this comfort carries a cost beyond electricity bills. Air-conditioners function by transferring heat from indoor spaces to the outdoors, releasing waste heat into an already warm urban environment. As temperatures rise, Hong Kong’s residents become increasingly dependent on cooling systems. But, the more the city relies on airconditioning, the more heat is released into the surrounding environment. This creates a vicious self-reinforcing cycle: the temporary solution to rising temperatures makes the underlying problem worse.

This is not just a local issue: Climate change has been increasing temperatures and making extreme heat more frequent. Hong Kong is particularly vulnerable to these effects because of its dense buildings, extensive concrete surfaces and limited green space. According to the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department1, air-conditioning accounted for approximately 30% of Hong Kong’s total electricity consumption in 2023. Meanwhile, the Hong Kong Observatory2 recorded 54 hot nights in 2025, which was the third highest annual total since records began in 1884. These figures show how heavily the city depends on cooling systems while facing increasingly persistent heat.

The problem becomes more serious within Hong Kong’s urban environment. Concrete buildings and paved surfaces absorb and retain heat at nature, while limited greenery reduces the

EMSD, 2025 Hong Kong Observatory, 2026

possibilities of natural cooling. Air-conditioning systems further contribute by releasing the heat from indoor spaces into already warm surrounding areas. Recent research conducted in Sai Ying Pun found that temperatures in urban street-canyons could rise by 1-3oC above the surrounding ambient temperatures during summertime, with air-conditioning exhaust and other human activities contributing to this warming (Huang et al., 20203). As outdoor temperatures increase, residents and businesses would require more cooling, potentially intensifying the urban heatisland effect. Therefore, this issue is not simply about individual electricity consumption, it is also about how Hong Kong designs and manages its urban environment.

Hong Kong needs a practical response addressing both cooling demand and outdoor heat. The government should adopt a two-pronged strategy focusing on building efficiency and public infrastructure. Together, these measures can reduce dependence on cooling systems while making the city more resilient to extreme heat.

The first prong would focus on improving buildings: The government should introduce stronger passive-cooling requirements for new developments and major renovations. These standards should encourage the construction of green roofs, improved insulation, external shading, and natural ventilation. Existing buildings should also receive financial incentives to retrofit outdated cooling systems with energy-efficient equipment. Simply asking residents to use less airconditioning would not address the buildings that trap heat in the first place, so, by designing buildings that can remain cooler naturally, Hong Kong can reduce electricity demand and the waste heat ejected by cooling systems. Buildings should be designed to prevent trapping excessive heat rather than relying entirely on machines to remove it.

Huang et al.

The second prong should focus on transforming public spaces. The government should establish a citywide urban cooling programme prioritising tree planting, shaded walkways and green infrastructure. Trees can provide shade and cool their surroundings through evapotranspiration, while green roofs and walls can reduce heat absorption. Public spaces should also incorporate shaded areas, allowing residents to not have to constantly seek refuge in air-conditioned spaces. This is particularly important for outdoor workers, elderly residents and people who cannot afford constant cooling. This prong is important as research on Hong Kong’s urban heat island found that residential cooling energy demand in urban planning areas could be up to 5 times higher than in rural areas (Liu et al., 20254), demonstrating why improving the urban environment is essential.

These reforms would be able to benefit both individuals and the wider community. Better building design could lower electricity bills and reduce dependence on cooling systems, while greener public spaces would improve residents’ everyday experience. More importantly, these changes would be able to address the unequal burden of extreme heat: People who work outdoors or live in poorly ventilated homes often have fewer opportunities to escape high temperatures. A cooler urban environment could then provide protection beyond those who can afford private cooling systems.

The era of treating air-conditioning as the only answer to rising temperatures has to end. Hong Kong must start redesigning the environment that has been worsening the problem. We must

Liu et al. 2025

demand greener buildings, shaded streets and smarter cooling strategies. It is time to break the heat cycle, not keep feeding it.

Beyond Technology: Building a Just and Sustainable City Imagine that I am a policymaker who has the responsibility of transforming the city into a sustainable, low-carbon society. Given the fact that our resources are limited, where should I start? Should I introduce a carbon tax immediately? Should I invest in renewable energy? Or should I reward those who protect the environment? Before taking this course, I believed that such climate issues could be solved through technological advancement. However, after a series of debates and discussion, I noticed that these problems may affect multiple sectors and social groups. Thus, I would need to draw the bigger picture of the issues and try to maximize the overall benefit. As a policymaker, one thing I want to invest in the most is renewable energy. According to the Institute for Energy Research (2026), fossil fuels still account for approximately 86%. Although renewable energy now is constantly growing, fossil fuels are still in the dominant position. Therefore, transforming the city into a renewable energy-based city may seem to be a simple answer to climate change. However, there is a major problem with this transformation, the cost. Let’s take wind power as an example, in order to develop such technology, we would need materials whose prices may rise due to increasing demand. Such price spikes could delay the deployment by 13% and increase the installation cost by $228 billion (Yuan et al., 2025). Thus, I realized that technology development can be limited by economic problems and here comes to our second problem: where should our funding come from? Funding is always a challenge for any public policy. The first thing that comes to my mind is a carbon tax. Introducing a carbon tax and establishing an emissions trading system can generate government revenue. According to the World Bank (2026), carbon pricing generated $107 billion in 2025. Thus, the government can use some of the revenue to invest in renewable energy and energy transition. Funding can also come from private corporations. In order to attract enterprises to invest, the government can ensure a stable regulatory environment and provide loan guarantees. By reducing uncertainty and market risks, private investors may be more willing to invest in the industry (International Energy Agency [IEA], 2025). However, introducing a carbon tax can lead companies to pass the costs on to customers, which

may increase the cost of living for the public (Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development [OECD] & United Nations Development Programme [UNDP], 2025). I realised that another issue I need to address is the system itself. Although the introduction of carbon pricing is to make those who pollute take responsibility, the burden can eventually be borne by the public due to the interconnected economic system. Merkle and Dolphin (2024) developed a mathematical model to examine how increased costs due to carbon tax could be passed on to customers. They found that the effect of carbon pricing towards household expenditure has a regressive impact in all 19 EU countries examined in 2020, which means households with lower income may face a greater relative financial burden. This is obviously not the purpose of such policy. I was surprised that a good intention can result in a totally different outcome. The policy designed to protect our environment may end up adding difficulties to those who are already financially vulnerable. As a policymaker, I started to ask myself a question: What is the point of creating a green city where people there can’t even afford their basic needs? Enforcing a carbon tax can indeed increase government revenue and boost energy transition but the consequences may include unfair distribution of financial burdens. Therefore, I propose a three-part policy. First, we introduce a carbon tax gradually, instead of putting a huge burden on companies and customers all of a sudden, which allows them to prepare and adapt to it. Second, we can provide subsidies to households with relatively lower income and those who suffer from climate change to ensure fair allocation of such revenue. Finally, we can invest the remaining funds in research and deployment of renewable energy. The implementation of these measures and the allocation of funds should remain flexible. essay.text:
Fifteen years ago, one in five black-faced spoonbills, a previously endangered waterbird species, wintered in Deep Bay. Today, that number has fallen to 4.4% (Hong Kong Bird Watching Society [HKBWS], 2026). A tagged spoonbill, A56, was tracked earlier this year to be moving among fishponds in Lok Ma Chau, San Tin, and Ma Tso Lung (HKBWS, 2026). As sea levels rise, ponds like these may become increasingly important refuges for waterbirds, though they are in areas covered by the Northern Metropolis plan (Wikramanayake et al., 2020; Civil Engineering and Development Department [CEDD], n.d.). The species is recovering globally, but over 60% of the population is concentrated at just a few wintering sites, making the wider wetland network crucial (HKBWS, 2026). Furthermore, climate change adds pressure as parts of Mai Po’s mudflats could be submerged by 2100 due to rising sea levels, leaving inland fishponds as the alternative habitat (Wikramanayake et al., 2020). Yet many of these privately-owned ponds are vulnerable to development (Wikramanayake et al., 2020). Under the Northern Metropolis plan, approximately 90 hectares of fishponds are planned to be filled, with their ecological function intended to be offset by a 338-hectare wetland park scaled back from 520 hectares and not due for completion until 2039 (Lin, 2024; Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, 2025, 2026). That is a local choice with global consequences. The solution I propose is that Hong Kong treat the fishponds as working climate refuges: protect the connected ponds most useful to spoonbills and other waterbirds, and pay operators to keep managing them. Together, these ponds could give waterbirds more places to feed and rest as coastal wetlands change, while the long-term payments would help support local fish

farming and recognize operators as partners in conservation, rather than leaving them to shoulder the costs alone. First, map which ponds A56 and the other waterbirds use by extending HKBWS’s existing surveys and tracking, before overlaying those routes with sea-level-rise projections. The Mai Po model suggests inland fishponds may be less exposed than coastal mudflats in some scenarios, so the evidence can be utilised to identify priority pond clusters (Wikramanayake et al., 2020). Next, offer operators multi-year payments to keep those ponds in active, wildlife-friendly use. There are existing management agreements which fund practices such as lowering pond water during harvest, and creating shallow feeding areas for waterbirds (Countryside Conservation Office, n.d.). That approach can be expanded in areas such as San Tin and Ma Tso Lung, while continuing to monitor bird use and pond conditions. Additionally, before approving development that removes habitat, require evidence that replacement wetlands are functioning and not just land that has been set aside. This is just one case in a wider pattern: climate change is shifting where species can live. Research found that species both on land and in ocean have shifted from lower to higher latitudes as the world warms (Costello et al., 2022), so protection designed for today’s map loses value as habitats move. One model projects climate-connectivity failure across 58% of protected land at 2°C warming, though this finding is debated (Parks et al., 2023; Gillingham & Thomas, 2023). For migratory spoonbills especially, connectivity is significant due to their dependence on the wetland chain, where losing one link can weaken the entire network (Wikramanayake et al., 2020). Adaptation should therefore keep habitats connected, track where animals go, and support people who manage those landscapes. For the reader, there are clear avenues to help as a citizen. For the vulnerable spoonbill species, choose local fish carrying HKBWS’s “Catch for Spoonbill” label, and learn more

about the initiative itself, which returns income to bird-friendly operators (HKBWS, n.d.). The Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) report for the Northern Link Spur Line is also open for public comment until 28 November 2026, and a short email to eiaocomment@epd.gov.hk could urge the Environmental Protection Department (EPD) to protect connected wetland habitat and promote transparent monitoring. Beyond spoonbill wetlands, support the wider issue of climate-driven habitat loss by volunteering with or donating to WWF-Hong Kong’s conservation work, and backing policies that cut emissions and protect connected habitats. In early 2026, tagged spoonbill A56 moved between ponds that are also lines on a planning map. When looking at landscapes, climate change raises two questions: what do we protect, and who pays? Addressing both is imperative to adaptation—protecting connections between habitats while distributing its costs fairly.

Fast Fashion and Climate Change: Ending Fast Fashion’s Damage

In Chile’s Atacama Desert, mountains of discarded clothing stretch across the sand. Many pieces still carry price tags. The weather is so dry, so the clothes cannot break down even after a decade. Locals burn these clothes, the toxic smoke from the fire directly harms the local community (Chambers, n.d.).

The same pattern appears worldwide. The fashion industry makes over 100 billion clothes every year (United Natiins Enviroment Programme, 2025). However, many of these clothes are never sold or are thrown away very quickly. This creates a huge amount of waste. In Hong Kong, the problem is visible. the city landfills the equivalent of 17,480 suitcases of textiles daily as people think the clothes are no longer trendy (Texfash, 2025). In addition, the problem is not just about waste the resources, the human cost is just as heavy. On April 24 2013, the Rana Plaza building, which had several garment factories producing clothing for global brands in Bangladesh. Over 1,100 people died during the case as the building collapsed. It brought international attention to the unsafe working environment in the fast fashion industry, which prioritizes low-cost production to meet the high demand for cheap clothing worldwide (Rich, 2023). Therefore, fast fashion damages both our planet and the people who make our clothes.

The solution is we need a new textiles economy system which we will stop making clothes that just follow the trends. Instead of designing clothes to follow the short-lived trends, we design them to keep them in use longer and recycle them after we use them. The Ellen MacArthur Foundation shows that large amounts of non renewable resources are extracted to

produce clothes that are often used for only a short time, after which the materials are mostly sent to landfill or incinerated so this new system is very important that it can help us stop wasting money and natural resources (Ellen MacArthur Foundation, 2017). Today, the fashion industry loses more than 500 billion US dollars every year through the fast fashion trendy. A circular economy approach captures this value and turns waste into useful.

This system connect is three ways. First, changes how we design clothes. Companies design stronger, repairable garments from the start. Second, changes how we use clothes. We can rent clothes, buy second-hand, or keep old clothes instead of buying new ones. Third, build the infrastructure to turn old textiles back into new fibre instead of sending them to landfill. We need new machines and systems to turn old clothes into new fabric. In Hong Kong these steps are practical. The Hong Kong government and local community groups can collaborate together which The government can fund sorting to build recycling factories ; local community groups can teach people how to recycle and repair clothes, more collection bins can be placed in every district and shops can offer take back schemes to customers with discounts These actions can reduce the waste in landfills and create local jobs.

Everyone having benefits for refusing the fast fashion. The environment receives less waste in landfills and less pollution. Workers face fewer dangerous like Rana Plaza as the production slows and the standard rise. Citizens spend less over time by owning fewer and better pieces. Local businesses gain new jobs opportunities in recycling and repair.

Actions can start from today. Before buying something new, ask three simple questions: Do I really need this? Do I already have something similar this? Will I wear this at least 30 times?

If the answer is no, walk away. Also, try to buy second-hand clothes when possible and repair your old clothes instead of throwing them away you can find a clothes recycling bin near your home. Every small action helps change the system.

In conclusion, fast fashion has already left scars in our planet. We must change how we make and use clothes. From the desert in Chile to the landfills in Hong Kong, we can all make a difference. CCGL9065 Our Response to Climate Change: Hong Kong 2100 Final Reflective Essay

The fishing net that came up with empty of fish

Imagine yourself as a fisherman. On a humid morning, you hauled his net and found more plastics stuck in it than fishes. Bottles, food wrappers, fragments of white styrofoam from oyster rafts and tangled fishing lines filled the mesh. You sorted the catch by hand, tossing everything you caught back into the sea that once fed your family. That quiet moment is no longer rare along Hong Kong’s coastline. The food, textiles, and industry pollution we’ve produced have eventually flowed into the sea, causing irreversible damage to our ocean. The Ocean absorbs 29-30% of the carbon dioxide we emit from daily life. (UN News, 2026; Global Carbon Project, 2025). Climate change has reduced the ocean carbon absorption capacity, warmer surface water reduces solubility and lowers Ocean PH which harms shellbuilding marine life and ecosystems. At the same time, we are also loading the ocean with debris. Microplastics produced by humans also appeared at several coastal sites in Hong Kong, with concentration highest at river mouths and near urban discharges. (Lo et al.,2025). Over 60 percent of marine litter collected on local shores originated from land-based activities, and citizens in Hong Kong use approximately 5million plastic bottles everyday which further intensified ocean pollution.(Lee et al., 2024) These numbers are not abstract. Across the semester we saw how different systems create these pressures: Everyday convenient food packaging, takeaway containers, and aquaculture floats enters drains and rivers; types of particles and road dusts washed off streets during rain, synthetic microfibres from fabric escape from washing machine and enters the sewage systems, industrial production, energy systems and transport that generated particles and carbon emissions. Once these pollutants enter the water, they do not disappear. They entangle and choke ocean animals, damaging marine life habitats. When we pollute the ocean, we are not only dirtying the water; we are damaging the living systems that sustain fisheries, coastal protection, and the climate itself.The ocean sits at the end of these chains. What begins as a packaging decision or a fast-fashion purchase ends in our fishing net. Stopping the flow of plastic and waste is an act of protecting the ocean’s ability to protect us. A concrete response already exists. Strengthening mandatory extended producer responsibility would require companies that place packaging and bottles on the market to finance collection, recycling and redesign. (GovHK,2026; Environment Bureau, 2021) This shifts the cost upstream, motivating producers to create incentives for less wasteful designs. We citizens also hold the mighty power; The reusable water bottle we carry, the restaurants

that use less packaging or the takeaway containers we refuse to take, the microfibre-catching laundry bags we use ,fast fashion purchases we avoid when possible, the volunteering actions like harbour clean up we join can significantly lower the environmental burden. These actions matter urgently because everyday delay will allow more plastic to accumulate in the ocean. As larger pieces of plastics break down, more microplastics enter the food chain, first into plankton then into big fishes, last it goes back into us. If we humans do not want to consume microplastics and polluted waste, then why should marine life be forced into ? In fact, we depend on the ocean far more than we admit, as it regulates the climate, supports the fishing industry, protects the coastline and sustains the web of life that makes our own survival possible. When we pollute, we are not damaging something abstract, but we are the ones who weaken the ocean system that keeps us alive. Being considerate is not only showing kindness to marine life but also shows a responsibility towards ourselves and towards those who might bear the consequences after us. However, change does not always start with policies and legislation, it often begins with a quiet decision like refusing to use plastic bags, bottles, containers and initiating climate actions like collecting litter that would otherwise drift out to the sea. We all know the ways to combat climate change, yet our laziness always hinders us from taking our first step. The ocean has carried us for generations, it is the time for us to carry some responsibilities in return. Imagine a different morning in Sai Kung once again. You haul in your net and find fish that move vividly, instead of bottles and broken styrofoam. The weight in the hands feels similar again. Relief mixes with quiet gratitude. This moment is not impossible, and it depends on the choice we make now.

Who Pays for Hong Kong’s Climate Goals?

essay.text:
Consider the owner of a cha chan teng in Sham Shui Po, who has just opened her electricity bill and is wondering if a new carbon price will impact her shop in the coming month due to the many appliances she uses. Her question is essentially about the cost associated with electricity use, given that electricity generation contributed roughly 61% of Hong Kong's carbon emissions in 2024 (Hong Kong SAR Government, n.d.) – but it really speaks to the fundamental question: who pays for Hong Kong's climate objectives? Hong Kong intends to achieve carbon neutrality before 2050, while achieving a 50% emissions reduction from 2005 levels by 2035 (Hong Kong SAR Government, n.d.). There will be some kind of cost distribution in Hong Kong, among government, businesses and households. Similarly, through much of this course, the same tension was revealed, whether it was for affordable fashion or for ocean conservation and livelihoods. At the end of these cases, the strongest arguments defended both the people (by helping to cover some costs) and climate action goals. Unlike other instruments of change, a carbon tax confronts this issue head-on. I believe that a policy of a carbon pricing scheme on fossil fuel-based emissions would work best if a carbon tax was coupled with a reasonable, fair dividend of that cost back to individuals as well. Evidence that pricing has an effect is strong; Andersson (2019) found that both the carbon tax and tax on transport fuel in Sweden decreased transport emissions by nearly 11% relative to a simulated control group, suggesting that pricing works most effectively with viable substitution alternatives to the taxed activity. Murray and Rivers (2015) also studied the impact of British Columbia's tax and found emissions cut approximately between 5 and 15%, with almost no measurable effect on overall economic activity. Design is just as important, if not more important, than headline rates. British Columbia made its carbon tax revenue neutral; gave each resident a Climate Action Credit in the form of a 100(30 for children) annual payment (Province of British Columbia, 2008). It was also noted that trust in a policy is difficult to build; the federal fuel charge in Canada had a monthly rebate system but still was removed on 1 April 2025 (Government of Canada, 2025). Carattini et al. (2018) identified fears about the costs, fairness, and the use of revenue as barriers to adoption of climate policy and therefore I believe that transparency should be a part of the policy design process. In Hong Kong, I envision the policy of the lowest possible price on carbon, increasing it at a measured pace over many years, and targeting the lowest income households through an efficient government channel, along with grants to small stores who purchase qualifying energy efficient equipment.

The immediate advantage would go to people living on the lowest incomes and small businesses, as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2023) suggests that the money from carbon pricing could be used to support poor households. Everyone benefits from a policy that results in lower emissions and is easy to trust. You can start taking action now without the need to wait for a proposal for a new carbon policy; whenever someone puts forward a carbon policy, consider asking three questions: who will pay? Who will be protected? Who will evaluate the outcome? Furthermore, you can get in touch with your Legislative Council member asking that the carbon pricing proposal contain a plan detailing how the generated money will be used. In the instance of the café owner, that would mean an opportunity to receive a dividend to reduce her expenditure and possibly receive an investment grant towards the purchase of a power-saving fridge. People can only feel inspired and motivated if the carbon price appears to relate directly to them. If the café owner knows that the proceeds will return to her and that she can have access to some capital investment for equipment improvements, then her engagement in climate action will transition from being viewed as something punitive towards being considered an action that she may want to take part in.

From a Pop-Up to a Habit: Rethinking Clothing Reuse

The shirt was still folded when I found it, tag half torn. I purchased this shirt one year ago for one event and only wore it once. Now it was a problem to be solved because the dress is so big that it fills a quarter of the suitcase. When I need to move out, I have no way to take it with me. I began to consider clothing swap. After browsing the relevant information, I noticed that HKU held a Clothing Swap Pop-up Market on 4 and 5 October 2023.Those dates raise a question on my mind. If a student realized the following week that they needed a jacket or if a student like me who need such an event found that the recent event was years ago. This was not necessarily HKU‘s only clothing swap event, but the gap matters. There is a difference between pop-up event and regular event.

I used to locate climate responsibility inside my own head. I asked myself whether to buy before purchase. I rarely asked the harder question such as if the product is not new, what other option is just as convenient? Restraint was my whole strategy and my answer depended entirely on willpower.

The third week's case study on denim fabric demonstrates that the story of clothing does not begin at the point of purchase. In fact, it involves cotton fields, dyeing factories, cargo ships, and the ownership stage. If we only consider the destination of clothing, we cannot understand its complete history. Research shows that compared to recycling, reusing clothes can increase environmental benefits. Most of the benefits of reusing clothes come from not producing new products (Sandin & Peters, 2018). Collecting 100 garments for reuse can reduce the global warming impact of a cotton T-shirt by 14% (Farrant et al., 2010). When buying second-hand clothes, the climate impact can be reduced by up to 42% each time they are worn (Klooster et al., 2024). This reframed my drawer. Cleaning out the drawer responsibly and buying new clothes did not shrink my carbon footprint. Only by allowing the shirts to continue circulating could the footprint potentially be reduced. Although the campus pilot program was small, it still managed to avoid some of the burdens associated with producing new clothes.

Week 6 explains why willpower alone fails. People choose sustainable options when they are convenient and predictable. Even eco-minded students rarely share or swap clothes without an effortless setup, otherwise defaulting back to shopping apps (Hobson & O'Byrne, 2024). Thus, I stopped asking how to be a more disciplined consumer and started asking who can reshape the conditions for our next choice.

Here is a proposal, a monthly campus clothing swap pilot even on a small scale could make a real difference. Student clubs can simply book a regular time and spot, so everyone knows where to go. To keep things running smoothly without getting overly complicated, a few basic ground rules would help. For starters, we need to pay attention to fabric quality since blended fibers are notoriously tough to recycle down the line (Chen et al., 2021). Beyond that, anyone can grab something they like even if they didn't bring anything to swap, and lining up a local charity beforehand takes care of whatever's left over at the end.

I will not pretend this solves climate change. The exchange room cannot reform the supply chain, and the number of participants also fails to demonstrate any changes in emissions. The clothing exchange process may also encounter some real conflicts, such as concerns about hygiene, mismatches in sizes, and logistics issues regarding the transportation of clothes between individuals (Armouch et al., 2024; Lang & Zhang, 2019). Therefore, the pilot must measure whether swaps truly replace new purchases rather than merely adding clutter. The reason is that estimates suggest every five second-hand acquisitions replace only about three new purchases (Sandin & Peters, 2018; Gaeta & Silvestri, 2026).

This shirt has been sent away by me now. I posted its details online and gave it to a friend of mine because she told me she needed this one to participate in the same one-time event as the one I bought before. The goal is not to turn every day into a market. It is to build a campus where the sustainable choice is the easy one.

portfolios.title: Can You Still See Nature?

essay.text:
When was the last time you truly listened to the wind moving through the leaves, or noticed the intricate veins of a fallen leaf? For most of us living in dense urban jungles, the answer is far too long ago. We have traded the smell of damp soil for filtered air, and the chorus of insects for the hum of air conditioning. In doing so, we have lost our ecological literacy. We desperately want to "save the environment," but we have forgotten how to even see it. True environmental action does not begin in a policy room; it begins at eye level with a seedling. To solve the overarching environmental crisis, we must stop treating nature as an abstract problem and start experiencing it as a home to be cherished.

The consequences of this disconnect are profound. Overarching environmental issues—from biodiversity collapse to extreme weather—are essentially the symptoms of a system we no longer understand. Because of this lack of true understanding, these issues are easily re-enchanted in our minds, unintentionally or deliberately, by those with vested interests. Some groups deliberately shift the focus to protect their own agendas, blocking us from the truth. Let me show you something surprising: we passionately defend the rainforest, yet ignore that marine phytoplankton—organisms we cannot even see—generate over half of the oxygen we breathe. We quantify our progress in GDP, completely ignoring the silent massacre of biodiversity happening at a rate 1,000 times faster than natural extinction. This is the reality of our blind spots. We cannot simply react with panic or apply generic fixes; only when we truly comprehend exactly what is unfolding within our natural environment can we identify the genuinely appropriate and effective solutions. We cannot solve a crisis we barely comprehend.

I am not telling these stories to shout hollow slogans, but as reminders of what we have long ignored. Imagine a Sunday morning in Hong Kong. An elderly resident, Mr. Chan, used to watch sparrows nest in the cracks of his aging tenement building. When a glass high-rise replaced it, the birds vanished. He felt a quiet grief, even without knowing the term "biodiversity loss." Then, a group of students visited. They didn't lecture him with abstract data; they sat with him, opened a citizen science app, and helped him record the few remaining sparrows in a nearby park. Suddenly, his local knowledge had value. He became the neighborhood's unofficial bird guardian. This is the power of placebased education: it turns a distant, overwhelming issue into a personal, tangible one.

Fostering this eco-friendly awareness is not a task reserved for policymakers; it is a call to action for all of us. First, we can demand that schools break down the walls of the classroom. Instead of merely analyzing data on screens, we can petition to integrate "ecological literacy" into the curriculum, turning local parks into living laboratories. Second, we can actively participate in citizen science. By using mobile apps to document local flora and fauna—like the declining urban sparrows (Ming Pao, 2024)—ordinary citizens can contribute verifiable data to biodiversity databases. The overarching environmental crisis will not be solved in a sterile laboratory or a distant colony. It will be solved in the quiet moments when a city dweller touches damp soil or pauses to listen to the wind. This is a deeply hopeful endeavor. Every time we step outside to identify a native plant or record a local bird, we are not just collecting data; we are actively restoring our bond with the living world. Such profound understanding and intimate connection will naturally translate into a powerful, collective force—one that can drive real systemic change and healing our planet. We do not need to escape this planet to find paradise; we need to notice the one still blooming outside our

windows. Let us step away from our screens and walk out into the wild corners of our neighborhoods.

The uncounted emissions beyond the boundary

Living in Hong Kong, my life is full of imported goods, like electronics from America, beef from Australia and clothes from China. They are produced outside Hong Kong, producing CO2 somewhere else. Hong Kong residents enjoy them while being proud of low emission of CO2 in Hong Kong, 4.35 tonnes in 2024 (Our World in Data, n.d.-a), less than a third of that in the US. If all the emissions produced by the products we consume were really counted back to us, this figure would become 19.9 tonnes (Our World in Data, n.d.-b), even higher than the US’s. Our lifestyle would seem no longer environmentally friendly.

This is not because the government lies to us. According to the rule of UNFCCC (IPCC, 2006), the government should count the fuel that burns inside the country only so that emissions will not be double counted. It flatters Hong Kong where 61% of the emissions is from electricity, 18% from transport and 8% from waste and almost nothing from manufacturing as the factories are elsewhere (Environment and Ecology Bureau, 2026). And researchers in Hong Kong estimate that 62% consumption-based emissions here comes from imports (Yau et al., 2018).

This means Hong Kong’s emission figure is technically accurate but materially misleading as a large amount of the emissions which support our life occurs beyond our territorial boundary. When Hong Kong celebrates the low emission in Hong Kong, the pollution related to the consumption is experienced by communities beyond its border.

So I think the solution is publishing the two figures in the same year in the same format. One figure is calculated in the previous way the government did in the past, while the other one should be based on consumption. They work together to make a comparison, showing that importing more is just a cheap but not the best way to make Hong Kong greener. And a new standard of progress in environment protection would be shrinking the gap between the two figures. This method has zero political cost as no one is forced to reduce the emissions but can help more people realize the hidden carbon account behind everyday consumption of imports.

This method has had precedents in the UK. Defra has published the UK’s carbon footprint with the territorial emissions every year since 2012. According to the figures, UK territorial emissions fell 50% between 1996 and 2023, while its footprint fell 15%, and the share of its footprint from imports rose from 31% to 53% (Defra, 2026). The second figure punctures the environmentally-friendly situation shown by the first one. But there may be a problem that the consumption-based estimates are unstable, as the re-exports can be counted twice. Defra’s response to this objection is publishing its assumptions and revisions. Hong Kong could do the same thing. An imperfect estimate is better than nothing.

If Hong Kong government publishes these two figures in the same year, its standing as a green city would change. Hong Kong looked clean partly because the emissions happen somewhere else. This fact sounds uncomfortable but it should be accepted, as Hong Kong promised to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050, with an absolute cut against 2005 meanwhile (Environment and Ecology Bureau, n.d.). Only the use of consumer-side accounting can show Hong Kong has really reduced carbon dioxide emissions instead of transferring emissions to other places. And this will benefit and give an example to other port cities like Singapore, Rotterdam and Dubai if Hong Kong becomes the first to publish both figures.

For us, except keeping the green and environmentally friendly lifestyle, we can start a small and specific action today. According to the Code on Access to Information (Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, n.d.), any member of the public can ask a government bureau for the information it holds. One request to the Environment and Ecology Bureau for a consumption-based estimate figure covering the same year is enough to draw attention. The government may still consider whether to release the data, but each request makes the next one harder to refuse.

Before taking this course, I did not realize that where the boundary draw will changes the answer, and accurate facts can also be misleading. I still believe the figure 4.35 tonnes published by the government, but before I become proud of this figure, I will consider the cost it brings to other regions.

Protect Hong Kong’s Corals Before the Boat Leaves

essay.text:
Protecting Hong Kong’s Corals Before the Boat Leaves

When I went diving a few months ago in Sai Kung, I paid little attention to the corals. Hong Kong’s 2024 coral bleaching event reminds me of that diving experience. Anchoring near coral communities would cause more damage to those already suffering from heat stress (Flynn & Forrester, 2019). It makes me wonder if a shared map before departure could help boat operators to choose the stop point to avoid adding to the stress on recovering corals.

Hong Kong’s 2024 Coral Bleaching Event

Coral bleaching is a process in which coral turns white due to changes in conditions like temperature, light, or nutrients (National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration [NOAA], 2026). Heat stress can cause corals to expel symbiotic algae that live in corals’ tissues. The bleaching could be improved if the stress is relieved.  Ocean warming is making marine heatwaves more frequent and intense on a global scale, which brings a higher risk of mass coral bleaching (Cooley et al., 2022). Hong Kong Reef Check (HKRC)’s 2024 survey found that coral bleaching occurred in 13 of 33 tested sites (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department [AFCD], 2024). A joint survey linked the July 2024 coral bleaching event to sustained high seawater temperatures (AFCD, 2025). Follow-up surveys found that corals at most affected sites were gradually recovering (AFCD, 2024). What could we do to protect corals during the recovery period?

Course Perspectives on Local Marine Conservation

The Week 8 case study shows that Hong Kong’s trawling ban brought about signs of recovery in some marine communities, though the results varied across different sites. It provides a perspective for thinking about this question: reducing one type of human stress can lead to improvement. During the recovery period, one of the main external stresses is damage caused by the ship’s anchor. Reducing anchoring in the recovering coral would help. The Week 10 discussion of cause-and-effect chains helped me understand that when surveyors discover bleached coral, they should update the information to boat operators. The operators could then adjust their anchoring position to reduce the possibility of anchoring near the injured coral community.

Proposed Pre-Departure Anchoring Advisory

A small pilot program could be launched in Sai Kung for dive boats heading to Sharp Island. When surveyors confirm coral bleaching near the island, the AFCD could work with local boat and dive operators by labelling the areas where bleaching has been confirmed on a shared map. It should include affected areas, current no-anchoring zones and confirmed alternative mooring points. AFCD could date each version and publish it in operators’ group chat, with a QR code linking to the latest version of the map. Boat operators should check the updated map before departure. If all suitable mooring spots are unavailable, operators should change dive sites or reschedule before departure. Sharing the map at this stage could give operators time to change their plan before leaving the dock.

Pilot Evaluation

However, if several operators choose the same alternative dive site, this guide could shift the anchoring pressure from Sharp Island to a nearby place. In this case, the pilot needs to track where the boat will anchor after changing plans. According to a survey in the British Virgin Islands, more boats choose sites with mooring buoys, which caused the density of boats anchored on coral reefs to become roughly half compared with sites without moorings (Forrester, 2020). Therefore, in Sai Kung’s pilot, AFCD should record the number of both total visiting boats and those anchored near corals at Sharp Island and nearby alternative sites, respectively. This would help in judging whether the advisory reduces anchoring around stressed corals or transfers the pressure to another bay.

Before booking my next dive in Sai Kung, I would ask where the boat plans to stop and whether it needs to anchor. A map shared before departure could make it easier for boat operators to choose a suitable stop point that would not damage the recovering corals.

Conclusion

In conclusion, anchoring would add more stress on corals that already suffer from heat stress. The Sai Kung pilot uses the coral monitoring results in planning the dive trips. It allows boat operators to know where they should avoid anchoring before departure and select a suitable alternative stop point. It could reduce avoidable damage to corals around Sharp Island during the bleaching recovery period.

essay.text:
Powering the Skyline From Within: A Bio-Urban Blueprint for Hong Kong 2100 Introduction A high-density global megacity with over 85% population residing in urban cores, that is Hong Kong in 2100. For decades, we have assumed that nature can endlessly absorb our industrial expansion under the “Abundance Mindset”. While the Anthropocene Extinction continues, tech companies like SpaceX spend billions on space tourism and Mars colonization to search for alternatives. To address 2100 Hong Kong, the central debate is whether to rely on external supply chains or build our own urban resilience. My stance is unequivocal: Climate resilience cannot be imported, and it is high time to abandon our energy-lazy dependency model while generating a localized bio-urban grid. The Spectacle Facts: While local renewables currently generate less than 1% of Hong Kong’s grid electricity due to land constraints, the potential is massive. These include rooftop solar installations, building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) and offshore wind developments across South China Sea marine territory, which adding up could cover up to 48% of our urban energy demand. However, Hong Kong chooses to rely on cross-border nuclear imports (Daya Bay power plant) for roughly 25% of its zero-carbon demand. Human Story: Behind every light switch in our high-rises lies a direct connection to power imported from across the border. When extreme climate events provoke cross-border supply shocks, wealthy districts weather the shock through automated generator systems. Yet, the burden lies on frontline workers trapped in high-density buildings and small business owners watching their refrigeration melt away under surging prices. Stakes: Importing our power offers immediate convenience at a heavy long-term cost. It limits domestic clean-energy innovation, hinders local job creation and hands control of our energy security to outside forces. When we outsource our electricity, we outsource our accountability. Hong Kong must break free from energy dependency and build self-sufficient local energy systems. Counterarguments

Pro-development perspectives frequently argue that cross-border bulk imports are cheaper, faster and require zero local land. They reckon that installing local micro-grids across thousands of skyscrapers costs too much. However, this objection depends on the “Doubt Machine” playbook. Just like tobacco corporations spent decades manufacturing uncertainty to delay structural reform, claiming that “local renewables are impossible in high-density cities” is simply an excuse to protect major power suppliers. Relying on cross-border power as a permanent fix locks the city into long-term systemic risk while suppressing local technological opportunities. Systems Thinking and the “Duck Curve” To ensure the bio-urban solution operates feasibly in the real world, systems thinking must be applied. Solar power alone is never enough. Its intermittency leads directly to the "Duck Curve" phenomenon, creating serious grid instability during peak consumption hours. Our 2100 response shifts from an industrial model that manufactures waste, to a regenerate architecture that grows energy. Hong Kong should establish a comprehensive policy framework spanning structural prevention and economic recovery. Under prevention guidelines of the Housing Bureau and EMSD, the government should mandate BIPV and micro-grid battery storage across all commercial towers and public housing estates. Pairing these renewable setups with municipal waste-to-energy facilities produces a continuous and decentralized power base without relying on backup fossil-fuel plants. Carbon tax revenues must be funneled into a targeted SME Green Capital Grant. This guarantees small business owners and vulnerable households’ direct funding and retraining support, ensuring no one is left behind as Hong Kong pivots to clean energy. Conclusion We cannot solve our 2100 climate challenges with the same short-term thinking that created them. As said by Buckminster Fuller, our goal must be to make the world work for 100% of humanity through spontaneous cooperation without ecological offense. Upgrading Hong Kong’s power grid enables high-rises to shift from passive energy consumers to key drivers of urban resilience. We do not need to escape to Mars to find a sustainable future; we must make our own skyline bloom.

Why Indonesia’s Karhutla Crisis Demands Prevention, Not Just Firefighting

Growing up in Indonesia, the dry season felt normal, until you realize what comes with it. Since

July 2026, alongside the dry season, severe forest and land fires (karhutla) have spread across

Sumatra and Kalimantan, choking not only Indonesian communities but also Singapore and

Malaysia. By mid-November, estimated carbon emissions approached 200 million tonnes

(Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, 2026), and toxic haze caused an estimated 3,560

air-pollution deaths in Indonesia in September alone (ABC News, 2026).

Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (2026) reported that Indonesia's September 2026

fire emissions were the third-highest on record, surpassed only by 2015 and 2019. Despite past

restoration efforts, recurring fires remain a severe regional public health crisis as smoke travels

hundreds of kilometres (Grosvenor et al., 2024). SCMP’s Asia desk (2026) reported welfare loss

of approximately US$1.97 billion in Malaysia from the 2026 karhutla, further contributing to an

estimated 1,700 deaths. Thus, what begins as a land-management problem in Indonesia ends up

as a global climate challenge.

The severity of Indonesia's forest and land fires (karhutla) crisis is closely connected to the

degradation of tropical peatlands. While peatlands help lock away enormous amounts of carbon,

deforestation and drainage for agricultural expansion make them increasingly vulnerable to

burning. Additionally, although El Niño-related drought intensifies fire seasons, human activities

create the underlying conditions for these disasters (Kiely et al., 2021).

As suggested by Hasan et al. (2026), to solve this issue, Indonesia must shift from reactive

firefighting towards preventive peatland management and strict penalties for illegal land

clearing. Therefore, I propose a strategy built around three priorities: peatland restoration,

community participation, and corporate accountability.

First, the government should prioritize restoring degraded peatlands through rewetting. Existing

canals that were dug to drain peatlands for agricultural purposes (drainage canals) lower

groundwater levels, allowing peat to dry and become highly flammable. Blocking these canals

can restore water levels and reduce fire risk. Kiely et al. (2021) support this, estimating that

completing the planned restoration of 2.49 million hectares of degraded peatland could have

reduced the 2015 burned area by 6%, CO₂ emissions by 18%, and PM₂.₅ emissions by 24%.

However, it is important that restoration considers existing land rights and the livelihoods of

communities dependent on these landscapes.

Second, local communities must become active participants in fire prevention. Government-led

enforcement alone cannot effectively monitor every vulnerable area. Communities should

receive training, equipment, and financial support to establish village-level fire monitoring and

prevention teams. They should also have access to sustainable agricultural alternatives that

reduce dependence on burning for land preparation. Carmenta et al. (2021) demonstrate that

successful fire prevention depends on combinations of interventions, including sanctions and

community awareness, rather than relying on a single measure, reflecting a systems-thinking

approach, where environmental protection cannot succeed without considering the economic

circumstances of those living within affected landscapes.

Third, Indonesia must strengthen corporate accountability. Companies operating in agriculture

and forestry should be required to demonstrate traceability throughout their supply chains and

face significant punishments for illegal burning and land degradation. Governments should

enforce existing environmental regulations more strictly, while international buyers should

prioritise suppliers with verified sustainable practices. Global demand for agricultural

commodities should not come at the expense of irreplaceable ecosystems.

These measures would not only benefit Indonesia, but others as well. Whereas local communities

would experience cleaner air, fewer health risks, and more secure livelihoods, neighboring

countries would benefit from reduced greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution. Kiely et al.

(2021) estimated that peatland restoration could have generated US$8.4 billion in economic

savings across major Indonesian fire events between 2004 and 2015. Prevention is therefore not

merely an environmental expense but an economically rational investment.

As consumers and members of an interconnected global economy, we can act today. Every

purchase we make sends a signal up the supply chain. So, choose certified sustainable products

when buying everyday groceries, cosmetics, and paper products. Look for sustainability

certifications, such as the Roundtable on Sustainable Palm Oil (RSPO) or Forest Stewardship

Council (FSC). Additionally, support community-led peatland restoration projects.

We must stop treating forest fires as inevitable and start treating their prevention as a shared

responsibility. The smoke of karhutla may feel miles away, yet our daily choices either feed the

fire or help put it out. Remember, no border can contain the smoke. Protect the peatlands, protect

the air, protect the planet.

portfolios.title: Invisible Data but Physical Storage Cost

essay.text:
Digital Sufficiency Alongside Corporate Accountability for Climate Resistance

Since the 21st century, the rapid growing internet has brought uncountable

convenience to the world, becoming an inseparable part of modern society. However, the

heavy cost behind this progress has gone unnoticed by the general public, being

overshadowed by the immense advantages. Our digital data, instead of being weightless and

invisible, is all stored in the physical network of data centres, at the price of staggering

amounts of electricity and water, contributing to the greenhouse effect at every moment. To

resolve this ongoing crisis, we must embrace digital sufficiency, a custom every citizen could

easily achieve through periodic checks on one's digital storage. Governments must also work

with companies, internalizing the true environmental costs so that sustainability is truly

considered and fostered.

The key mechanism behind the greenhouse gas emissions is a class of chemicals

called hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), which are used to cool cloud servers and prevent

overheating, acting as the backbone of the data centres' cooling system. Ironically, however,

once these gases trap heat and leak into the atmosphere, they act as notorious greenhouse

gases with a global warming potential up to 14,700 times that of carbon dioxide under the

IPCC's latest assessment, making it a huge contributor to the climate issue (Environmental

Investigation Agency, 2024). Besides this, resources used to maintain data centres were

massive. According to the International Energy Agency (2025), global data centres, in 2024,

consumed not only approximately 415 terawatt-hours of electricity, but also nearly 560

billion litres of water for the cooling process. The above statistics clearly showcase the

drastic amount of resources demanded to operate the whole physical cooling system, so as to

keep the virtual world functioning.

One of the existing "solutions" often used by tech companies as a response to such a

phenomenon was buying carbon offsets, financially funding green projects to compensate for

their emissions. But this was rather superficial, acting as a symptomatic treatment that

allowed companies to bypass tackling the root of the issue. As noted by Naoto in his audit

(2026), carbon offsets "become an alibi when they displace responsibility from the actual site

of environmental burden to an accounting mechanism," enabling corporations to claim

carbon neutrality while neglecting the continuous expansion in resource depletion. It neither

curbed the physical demand nor addressed the usage of HFC refrigerants; it only served as an

excuse that allowed the whole society to procrastinate on the unchanged greenhouse issue.

Genuine progress began only when we transferred our attention to measures that

directly affected energy consumption. As for individuals, the most straightforward yet

unnoticeable solution would be to adopt the mindset of digital sufficiency, to proactively

reduce digital reliance and virtual data. Some good practices were simply deleting duplicate

photos, discarding old emails, or any other events relevant to lowering storage. It might seem

insignificant, but the aggregate effect of millions of data removed would trigger a long-term

positive cascade that directly lessened the baseline demand for resources. As summarized by

Stanford Magazine, every 100 gigabytes of data would produce an annual 400 - 500 pounds

of carbon emissions, which was equivalent to powering an average home for 2 - 3 weeks

(Stanford Magazine, 2017, as cited in Varcho, 2026). Once everyone started periodically

cleaning redundant files or removing unused data, these seemingly minor habits accumulated

into a substantial drop in global electricity demand and carbon output, saving tons of energy

to support unavoidable powering.

However, individual efforts alone were insufficient under corporations' reckless

expansions to power the internet. Tech giants were rarely held accountable for the

environmental damages because the environmental impacts were often treated as external

costs that were imposed on the public and the planet rather than the companies themselves.

Without restrictions, companies would remain prioritizing their profits by expanding cloud

storage while ignoring environment fallouts, which became tragedy of commons. Addressing

such an issue required holding the firms accountable by making them internalize the cost of

their footprints. This was already in progress, with several U.S. states, including New Jersey

and Pennsylvania, done enforcing legislation that required formal submissions of reports for

data centres on their energy and water usage (Data Center Energy and Water Reporting Act,

2026). Other countries like Finland have also proposed similar legislation that demands

electricity consumption and water use (Dimou, 2026). We should promote these reporting to

become universal, facilitating transparency so that further actions could be precisely

calibrated, such as binding strict resource pricing and extraction caps. Only when companies

are forced to pay the true cost can they break away from the ongoing limitless expansion and

shift the entire focus back toward genuine sustainability.

Ultimately, everyone should be mindful of the obscured costs behind the virtual world

that not only causes a heavy resource burden but also contributes to the greenhouse effect. A

solution to ameliorate this phenomenon will be adopting digital sufficiency and combining it

with systemic corporate accountability, which will cease infinite extraction of resources and

draw back attention at sustainability.

Who Gets to Sleep? Cooler Homes for Hong Kong’s Hotter Nights

essay.text:
One hour of air-conditioning for a chance of eight hours of sound sleep. In a

windowless apartment in Hong Kong. Simon and Elaine Ho cooled the room before bed, just

to wake up a few hours later when the heat returned (Delmotte, 2023). If you cannot even

ensure sleep in your own apartment, can you really call it home? As Hong Kong’s nights get

hotter, we should urge housing authorities to check bedroom temperatures at night and how

heat transfers whenever an older building is due for a major renovation.

According to the Hong Kong Observatory, from 1995 to 2014, Hong Kong averaged

around 21 hot nights per year, when temperatures never went below 28°C (Hong Kong

Observatory, n.d.). As greenhouse gas emissions warm the planet, the number of hot nights

will only increase. According to HKO, under intermediate emission scenarios, the number of

hot nights will increase to a drastic 117 per year in 2081 to 2100 (Hong Kong Observatory,

n.d.)! For cities facing hotter nights, the IPCC pinpoints how heat flows into and out of

buildings as a starting point for change (Dodman et al., 2022, p. 924). Thus, Hong Kong

should consider the effects of housing conditions such as the thermal resistance, presence of

solar shading and ventilation of apartments on nighttime room temperature during

maintenance checks in older housing buildings.

The heat that woke up the Hos may have built up during the day. Housing materials

such as concrete, asphalt, and glass absorb heat and release it after sunset, contributing to the

urban heat island effect. A study on Hong Kong housing writes that “The synergetic effect of

UHI and heatwaves can further amplify urban overheating and increase building cooling

load” (Feng et al., 2026, Section 1, para. 3). The same study found that top floors generally

require more cooling than bottom floors in their simulations and identifies “the greater heat

gain through the exposed roof” (Feng et al., 2026, Section 4.1, para. 3) as the reason behind

this phenomenon. Following the lecture on democracy and capitalism’s shift from buildings

to decisions, we ask who decides on which aspect of the problem? Since occupants control

the air-conditioning, while the housing authority controls the roof. Residents should urge

authorities to inspect the roof before the next repair. If results confirm the roof as a major heat

source, test a reflective coating. Another separate experiment concludes that a reflective roof

averages a ceiling temperature 2°C lower than a conventional roof on sunny days(Zhao et al.,

2026). For other parts of the flat, match the repair to how heat enters and gets trapped. If

sunlight through the windows is the problem, ask for external shades. Likewise, if the room

stays hot even after outside air cooling, ask for an improved ventilation system (Dodman et

al., 2022, Section 6.3.5.2).

Some may argue that limited housing funds should prioritise urgent repairs instead,

and this deserves acknowledgement. Hence, without delaying essential repairs, we propose to

first test cooling improvements during scheduled maintenance, then weigh the extra cost

against potential electricity savings and better sleep quality, before wider implementation.

Moreover, the wider climate benefit of weakening the positive feedback loop that makes

air-conditioning more necessary should also be considered. In 2023, air-conditioning was

responsible for roughly 40% of Hong Kong’s residential electricity (Electrical and

Mechanical Services Department, 2025, p. 37). To generate the electricity needed, more fossil

fuels will be burned, releasing more carbon emissions and worsening warming. This

increases demand for air-conditioning, and the cycle repeats. This is a classic positive

feedback loop, a form of cascade effect, and our solution directly undermines it from the

source, weakening the cycle. Furthermore, if less air-conditioning is required after sunset, it

could ease the rise in electricity demand at night, flattening the steeper part of the Duck

Curve and making solar energy a more viable renewable energy source in Hong Kong. This

further weakens the feedback loop. Some may say one roof will barely affect climate change,

but if we stack the electricity savings across millions of flats in a city that heavily relies on

air-conditioning, we can cut the carbon emissions that make the world hotter for everyone.

That wider change can begin with the heat in your room. If your room stays hot after

sunset, ask your neighbours for opinions. Together, ask your estate office to investigate and

make nighttime heat part of their next repair plan. The next roof repair could mean a cooler

room and a lower electricity bill. The Hos’ story of one hour of air-conditioning for a mere

chance of eight hours of sleep should give Hong Kong more than enough of a reason to act. Is

asking for a home that lets you sleep at night really too much to ask for?
