portfolios.title: Saving the Colors of the Sea

essay.text:
In the summer of 2024, Mrs. Chan, a recreational diver from Sai Kung, went snorkeling into the clear waters near Sharp Island expecting to see the vibrant coral she had photographed for years. Instead, she saw large patches of coral turned ghostly white. For Mrs. Chan, coral bleaching was no longer a scientific term in a news report. It had become a painful reality beneath the waters of Hong Kong. Her experience reminds us that coral bleaching is not a distant environmental issue. It is happening here, now, and its consequences affect both nature and people.

Coral reefs are often called the “rainforests of the sea” because Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor, yet support roughly 25% of marine fish and other ocean species. Globally, coral bleaching has reached alarming levels. In 2025, scientists reported that about 84% of the world’s coral reef ecosystems had experienced bleaching stress, making it the most extensive bleaching event ever recorded. Rising ocean temperatures caused by climate change force corals to expel the algae that provide them with food and color, leaving behind pale white skeletons. Although Hong Kong is not famous for coral reefs like Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, it is home to diverse coral communities. Recent reports have shown that coral bleaching has appeared repeatedly in Hong Kong waters, increasing significantly in 2022 and again in 2024.

The most effective solution combines climate action, local coral conservation and innovative reef interventions. First, Hong Kong should scale up artificial reefs and 3D-printed clay reef tiles. Since 1996, Hong Kong has deployed artificial reefs, using sunken vessels and repurposed tires to rebuild habitats and boost fish populations. Currently, 3D-printed terracotta reef tiles are used, with their complex, porous surfaces that help coral fragments anchor securely to regrow. Moreover, this should be paired with nutrient management with coral probiotics to strengthen coral health directly in the ocean. Nutrient management techniques limit excess nitrogen and phosphorus to prevent harmful algal blooms, while coral probiotics introduce beneficial microbes that reshape the coral in situ to help corals withstand heat stress and disease. Together, physical reef tiles and biological treatment can help improve coral survival. Secondly, governments must reduce greenhouse gas emissions by accelerating the use of renewable energy and decreasing dependence on fossil fuels. Since warmer oceans are the primary cause of bleaching, addressing climate change would reduce temperature rise. Lastly, Hong Kong should expand coral monitoring and restoration programs. Marine scientists can identify areas most vulnerable to bleaching and focus conservation efforts there. Coral nurseries, where fragments of healthy coral are grown and later transplanted into damaged reefs, have already shown promise in many parts of the world. Such projects can increase reef resilience and speed up recovery after bleaching.

This solution works because it addresses both the cause and the symptoms of coral bleaching. Global climate policies reduce future warming, while local conservation projects protect reefs that still have a chance to recover. Rather than relying on a single strategy, this approach creates a coordinated response involving governments, scientists, and citizens.

The benefits of protecting coral reefs extend far beyond marine life. Healthy reefs support local fisheries by providing sheltered breeding, feeding, and nursery habitats where commercial fish species grow and replenish stocks. They also strengthen Hong Kong’s tourism sector by drawing divers, snorkelers, and eco-tourists to marine parks like Hoi Ha Wan and Sai Kung. Beyond these gains, reef structures buffer wave energy to reduce coastal erosion and storm damage, ensuring future generations gain a richer biodiversity and healthier oceans. Readers can contribute immediately by reducing their carbon footprint, choosing sustainable seafood, avoiding single-use plastics, and supporting marine conservation organizations.

Mrs. Chan’s dive near the Sharp Island proves that coral bleaching is already reshaping Hong Kong’s waters, yet reefs remain remarkably. With decisive climate action and science- backed restoration today, Hong Kong’s reefs can bloom again. Act now, and future generations will dive into thriving color instead of empty stone.

portfolios.title: Ocean Needs Both

essay.text:
On a hot 33-degree afternoon, a grandmother in a crowded Kwun Tong estate looks for the closest shaded park designated for redevelopment. The only cool outdoor spot she can find is the corridor of her building. Her family has been waiting years for a bigger apartment, but each new housing project seems to mean losing a small park. By the end of 2024, public rental applicants had been waiting an average of 5.3 years.(Hong Kong Housing Authority and Housing Department [HKHA], 2024). Her dilemma is the city-wide trade-off where housing and green space are treated as rivals.

This issue isn't just limited to Hong Kong. Around the world, cities are experiencing more intense heat waves, and the people most affected tend to be those who are economically and socially on the margins, living in crowded neighborhoods.(Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change [IPCC], 2022). In Hong Kong, the dense development, crowded public spaces, and lack of greenery make the city noticeably warmer than the countryside, increasing heat stress and energy consumption (Legislative Council Secretariat [LegCo], 2021). This issue hits home for many families who need stable, comfortable homes. Without enough shade, plants, and good ventilation, new housing estates risk repeating the same overheated and stressful living conditions that housing policies aim to improve.

The solution is to stop treating housing and green infrastructure as mutually exclusive and instead embed vertical and pocket green space inside every new residential development. Rooftop gardens, vertical plant walls, podium planting strips, ground-floor pocket parks and permeable paving can be designed into blocks from the outset, rather than added as decoration after the units are built.

This approach works because vegetation cools the built environment directly. Local measurements show that green roofs can reduce Hong Kong roof surface temperatures by roughly 18 to 26 degrees Celsius in August, while providing insulation that lowers cooling demand on upper floors (Architectural Services Department [ArchSD], 2007). More broadly, shaded vegetated surfaces can be 11 to 25 degrees Celsius cooler than unshaded ones, and trees cool pedestrian-level air more effectively than grass alone (LegCo, 2021). IPCC evidence likewise identifies urban greening and other nature-based solutions as mainstream, effective adaptation options that reduce urban heat and heat stress while improving resident well-being (IPCC, 2022).

Hong Kong should improve on its current rules instead of creating a new system. Right now, guidelines require at least 20% greenery for sites over 1,000 square meters and 30% for larger sites, with some flexibility for green features in the overall floor area (Development Bureau [DevB], 2011). These rules could be expanded to include rooftop gardens and green walls, with independent checks to make sure they are maintained and stay healthy after the buildings are finished. Developers who go beyond the green requirements can keep their floor area bonuses, and early consultation with residents and community groups can help ensure the designs meet the needs of families, seniors, and children, not just look good on paper. Importantly, this approach doesn’t mean building fewer homes; it means each building should have its own green spaces, on rooftops, walls, and ground level, to help keep the area cooler.

The primary beneficiaries are low-income public housing residents, elderly citizens and children, who spend the most time outdoors and are least able to rely on air conditioning at home. A greener estate means accessible shade, lower outdoor temperatures and healthier daily walking routes, alongside the new units the city urgently needs. The city also gains long-term climate resilience and reduced heat-related strain on public health services.

The next practical step anyone can take today is to be specific, not just symbolic. When the Housing Authority or Town Planning Board asks for public feedback on a nearby housing project, send in a written comment urging them to include rooftop gardens, green walls, and small pocket parks in the plans. Let them know that residents care about having both good homes and shaded outdoor spaces. One comment can show officials that it’s possible to have both, helping to move beyond the old idea that you have to choose between development and greenery.

Housing and green spaces don’t have to be at odds. Hong Kong can create safe, comfortable homes while also providing cool, green areas, if planners focus on integrating nature into their designs rather than forcing a choice between the two. A city that protects its residents should also protect the trees that help keep everyone cool.

Climate Media Literacy Programme

essay.text:
Every time I had a biomedical lab, I forgot to bring my lab coat. My professors repeatedly warned us that we would have to rent a disposable one for $10 if we forgot. I never remembered. During one biochemistry lab, my professor reminded us, but stated the reason like this: these disposable coats were made of plastic, so it takes thousands of years to degrade. She smiled and slowly added, "And it will harm sea turtles." Sometimes, one remembers something for a very long time because this thing has an inexplicable interesting anchor point for our memory. I do not know why, but that scene stayed with me. Since then, I never forgot to bring my lab coat. I think this is what a good pubic advocation should be like, changes are not motivated by moral shame, but people receiving vivid and persuasive opinions could conduct the sustainable behaviors in a easy and automatic way.

Climate change has long been surrounded by public controversy. The IPCC (2021) concluded that human influence on the warming of the atmosphere, ocean and land is unequivocal. Yet misleading communication can make this evidence seems uncertain. For example, some claims selectively talks about short-term weather variability while ignoring long-term climate trend. Furthermore, people's existing worldviews and political or economic beliefs can influence how they interpret climate information (Lewandowsky, 2021). Like me not recognizing the drawbacks of disposable coats on environments, if the public do not realize how their daily actions have already affected the climate, it’s not necessary to discuss any further adjustments.

The Hong Kong Observatory projects that annual maximum daily rainfall in 2081–2100 could be 28.1% higher than the 1995–2014 average under a very high emissions scenario (Hong Kong Observatory, n.d.). Our semester’s topics also connect: food and clothing depend on resource-intensive supply chains; buildings shape energy demand; and the oceans are affected by warming and pollution. What climate communication should do is to connect these systems to choices about consumption, energy and urban planning.

My experience has illustrated the concept of framing: the way information is selected and presented influences how people interpret an issue (Entman, 1993). We understood the importance of framing and might want to train young people’s critical analysis skills on certain claims. Therefore, a Climate Media Literacy Programme in Hong Kong schools and universities might raise awareness, where students construct their own frame by looking at some raw data, identify misleading framing, and learn to recruit and perform public engagement. Sometimes, action comes naturally after people have a deeper understanding of what climate change is about and what are the relationships of us with it.

Another useful strategy we can use in public advocation is that, people from different fields talk about their own experiences. Scientists can explain evidence, while local doctors, engineers, teachers, fishers and community workers connect climate risks to health, buildings, livelihoods and the sea. Effects of climate change that have infiltrated into their life are going to provide stronger perspectives to those who feel less interested. Public sessions should welcome questions about uncertainty, costs and policy trade-offs, rather than treating every concern as denial. Climate communication research recommends clear, repeated messages from a range of trusted and caring communicators (Maibach et al., 2023). A 2026 study further identifies clarity, sincerity and shared values as factors associated with trust in climate communicators (MacInnes et al., 2026).

Some people may say that this proposal has limits. Deep distrust are harder to be removed that we thought, and communication may have to combine with replace emissions cuts, resilient infrastructure or fair climate policy to achieve realistic progress. In a 12-country study of 6,816 participants, Spampatti et al. (2024) found almost no evidence that six inoculation strategies protected people from climate disinformation. No single lesson can create permanent “immunity”. The programme should therefore be evaluated over time, adapted to different audiences, collaborate transparent institutions, and enriched with accessible local evidence.

In my opinion, Hong Kong needs citizens who can question misleading posts, listen to different perspectives, discuss genuine trade-offs and conduct collective actions. The goal is to help them think critically, and act in an easier and evidential way.
